title: Generative Modeling of Stochastic Dynamics for Long-Time Evolution
summary: Exact stochastic equations for non-equilibrium dynamics are rarely accessible. We show that the long-time evolution of stochastic dynamics can be predicted from configuration pairs at a fixed short time lag, without knowledge of the equation of motion. Generative diffusion models learn the finite-time transition kernel from these pairs, and iterating it propagates the dynamics far beyond the training lag. For two-dimensional Model B, the diffusive dynamics of a conserved order parameter, the learned kernels reproduce dynamic critical scaling and self-similar $t^{1/3}$ coarsening. Agreement with direct simulations persists on lattices twice the largest training size and for initial ensembles absent from training. For driven colloids in a periodic optical potential, ten minutes of measured trajectories suffice to predict the particle current and mean passage time over the next twenty minutes within experimental uncertainty. Short-time observations thus contain the information needed to predict emergent non-equilibrium dynamics at much longer times.

AI.tldr: Short-time configuration pairs suffice to learn the finite-time transition kernel of stochastic dynamics via generative diffusion models; iterating the learned kernel predicts long-time non-equilibrium behavior, validated on Model B coarsening and driven colloids.
AI.motivation: Exact stochastic equations governing non-equilibrium dynamics are rarely accessible, so predicting long-time evolution typically requires knowledge of the underlying equation of motion, which is often unavailable.
AI.method: Generative diffusion models are trained on configuration pairs separated by a fixed short time lag to learn the finite-time transition kernel without the equation of motion. Iterating this kernel propagates the dynamics far beyond the training lag. Validation includes 2D Model B (conserved order parameter diffusive dynamics) and driven colloids in a periodic optical potential.
AI.result: For Model B, learned kernels reproduce dynamic critical scaling and self-similar t^{1/3} coarsening, with agreement persisting on lattices twice the largest training size and for initial ensembles absent from training. For driven colloids, ten minutes of measured trajectories predict particle current and mean passage time over the next twenty minutes within experimental uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Short-time observations contain the information needed to predict emergent non-equilibrium dynamics at much longer times, enabling equation-free long-time prediction from limited data.

title: Correlation Imaging via Hybrid Entanglement between Microwave Photons and Surface Acoustic Wave Phonons
summary: Establishing effective spatial correlations between distinct quantum fields is essential for multi-physics quantum sensing.~We here propose a correlation imaging approach based on the hybrid entanglement between microwave photons and microwave surface acoustic wave phonons generated via a superconducting quantum circuit.~At matched microwave frequencies, the five order-of-magnitude wavelength disparity between photons and phonons leads to a unique quantum entanglement resource, which allows the optimal field for probing an object to be distinct from that used for readout.~This resource enables two imaging modalities with giant spatial scaling: a $10^{-8}-10^{-6}$-fold demagnification of macroscopic object profiles onto microscopic phononic chips, and conversely, a $10^{4}-10^{6}$-fold magnification of microscopic object profiles into macroscopic photonic readout devices. By interfacing free-space long-wavelength microwaves with on-chip short-wavelength surface acoustic waves, our correlation imaging approach provides a general framework for cross-scale quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: Proposes a correlation imaging approach using hybrid microwave photon-phonon entanglement in a superconducting circuit, enabling cross-scale quantum sensing via distinct probe and readout fields.
AI.motivation: Effective spatial correlations between distinct quantum fields are essential for multi-physics quantum sensing. The five-order-of-magnitude wavelength disparity between microwave photons and surface acoustic wave phonons offers a unique resource for cross-scale imaging.
AI.method: Generate hybrid entanglement between microwave photons and microwave surface acoustic wave phonons using a superconducting quantum circuit, at matched microwave frequencies. This decouples the probing field from the readout field.
AI.result: Achieves two imaging modalities with giant spatial scaling: 10^-8 to 10^-6-fold demagnification of macroscopic object profiles onto microscopic phononic chips, and 10^4 to 10^6-fold magnification of microscopic object profiles into macroscopic photonic readout devices.
AI.conclusion: By interfacing free-space long-wavelength microwaves with on-chip short-wavelength surface acoustic waves, this correlation imaging approach provides a general framework for cross-scale quantum sensing.

title: Selective suppression of electronic orders via interlayer coupling in superconducting bilayer nickelate thin films
summary: The discovery of spin-density-wave (SDW) order in bilayer nickelates has intensified interest in its interplay with superconductivity. Unlike cuprates, where doping rapidly suppresses the Néel temperature, the SDW transition temperature ($T_{\mathrm{SDW}}$) in bilayer nickelates is robust against oxygen annealing and even increases under pressure. Here, we combine oxygen annealing with isovalent rare-earth ($A$-site) substitution to effectively apply $c$-axis uniaxial pressure, realizing superconducting bilayer nickelate films with $T_{\mathrm{SDW}}$ suppressed from 150 K to 70 K. Notably, while SDW order is weakened but remains, a second charge-like anisotropy order is completely eliminated in the superconducting state. Polarization-resolved O $K$-edge X-ray absorption and electronic structure calculations show that strengthened interlayer coupling reconstructs the Fermi surface and weakens the SDW. These findings, consistent with a spin-spinless stripe ground state, provide new insight into the mechanism of density wave formation and their interplay with superconductivity.

AI.tldr: Superconducting bilayer nickelate films were realized by combining oxygen annealing with isovalent rare-earth A-site substitution (effectively c-axis uniaxial pressure), suppressing T_SDW from 150 K to 70 K while eliminating a second charge-like anisotropy order and weakening but retaining SDW order.
AI.motivation: The discovery of spin-density-wave (SDW) order in bilayer nickelates has intensified interest in its interplay with superconductivity. Unlike cuprates, where doping rapidly suppresses the Néel temperature, T_SDW in bilayer nickelates is robust against oxygen annealing and even increases under pressure, making the mechanism of density wave formation and its relation to superconductivity unclear.
AI.method: The authors combine oxygen annealing with isovalent rare-earth (A-site) substitution to effectively apply c-axis uniaxial pressure, synthesizing superconducting bilayer nickelate films. They use polarization-resolved O K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy and electronic structure calculations to probe changes in interlayer coupling, Fermi surface reconstruction, and SDW behavior.
AI.result: T_SDW is suppressed from 150 K to 70 K. SDW order is weakened but persists, whereas a second charge-like anisotropy order is completely eliminated in the superconducting state. Strengthened interlayer coupling reconstructs the Fermi surface and weakens the SDW.
AI.conclusion: The findings are consistent with a spin-spinless stripe ground state and provide new insight into the mechanism of density wave formation and its interplay with superconductivity in bilayer nickelates.

title: From Quantized Hall Plateaus to Topological Surfaces: Quantum Capacitance as a Unifying Probe
summary: The quantum Hall effect, topological insulators and quantum capacitance are usually treated as distinct topics, yet they share a common thread. Bulk topology determines a protected boundary state, and quantum capacitance is one of the few electrostatic methods able to detect the density of states. This paper examines that connection. The integer quantum Hall effect showed that quantised boundary transport has a topological origin given by the Chern number, later extended to zero field in Z2 topological insulators with helical edge and Dirac surface states. Quantum capacitance, developed for two-dimensional electron gases, has since become a key technique for mapping the Landau level density of states underlying the quantum Hall effect and the linear Dirac density of states of topological surface states. This picture is complicated by self-consistent screening theory, which shows that the quantum Hall bulk splits into compressible and incompressible regions that shift with field. Local quantum capacitance measurements confirm that the bulk is not uniformly insulating across a quantised plateau, even though the plateau stays quantised. The paper argues that quantum capacitance is not a secondary feature of these phenomena but one of the clearest windows into the boundary density of states that topology imposes, and that it reveals the local, field-dependent nature of the insulating bulk assumption underlying the analogy between the quantum Hall effect and topological insulators.

AI.tldr: This paper links the quantum Hall effect, topological insulators, and quantum capacitance, arguing that capacitance is a key probe of the topological boundary density of states and reveals the locally field-dependent, non-uniform insulating bulk.
AI.motivation: The quantum Hall effect, topological insulators, and quantum capacitance are typically treated as separate subjects. The paper's motivation is to highlight their shared principle: bulk topology dictates a protected boundary state, and quantum capacitance is one of the few electrostatic techniques capable of detecting the associated density of states, so the connection deserves explicit examination.
AI.method: A conceptual synthesis: tracing how the integer quantum Hall effect's quantised boundary transport acquires a topological origin (Chern number), extended at zero field to Z2 topological insulators with helical edge and Dirac surface states; reviewing quantum capacitance's development from 2D electron gases into a tool for mapping Landau-level and linear Dirac densities of states; and incorporating self-consistent screening theory and local quantum capacitance measurements of compressible/incompressible bulk regions.
AI.result: Self-consistent screening theory shows the quantum Hall bulk splits into compressible and incompressible regions that shift with magnetic field, and local quantum capacitance measurements confirm the bulk is not uniformly insulating across a quantised plateau despite the plateau remaining quantised.
AI.conclusion: Quantum capacitance is not a secondary feature but one of the clearest windows into the boundary density of states imposed by topology. It also exposes the local, field-dependent nature of the insulating bulk assumption that underlies the analogy between the quantum Hall effect and topological insulators.

title: State-selective molecular orientation by vibrational Autler-Townes adiabatic passage
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures for manuscript; 7pages, 4 figures for supplemental material
summary: Control of molecular angular momentum orientation enables state-resolved studies of molecular interactions and provides a basis for quantum information processing. Here we propose all-optical Autler-Townes state-selective adiabatic passage (ASAP) to prepare molecules in a single $|J,M\rangle$ sublevel. An Autler-Townes branch created by a strong coupling field is selectively populated and adiabatically mapped onto the target vibrational state. We resolve detuning-dependent rovibrational Autler-Townes splitting in $^{13}$CO$_2$, establishing the spectroscopic basis for the selective excitation of the target dressed branch. The density-matrix model calibrated by these spectra predicts transfer approaching 90\%. The scheme can exploit millisecond vibrational radiative lifetimes within the electronic ground state and extend to polar and nonpolar molecules with infrared-active vibrational modes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes all-optical Autler-Townes state-selective adiabatic passage (ASAP) to prepare molecules in a single |J,M> sublevel, demonstrated via detuning-dependent rovibrational Autler-Townes splitting in 13CO2 with predicted transfer approaching 90%.
AI.motivation: Controlling molecular angular momentum orientation enables state-resolved studies of molecular interactions and provides a basis for quantum information processing. However, preparing molecules in a single |J,M> sublevel remains a challenge.
AI.method: An all-optical Autler-Townes state-selective adiabatic passage (ASAP) is proposed. A strong coupling field creates an Autler-Townes branch, which is selectively populated and adiabatically mapped onto the target vibrational state. Detuning-dependent rovibrational Autler-Townes splitting is resolved in 13CO2 to establish the spectroscopic basis for selective excitation of the target dressed branch. A density-matrix model is calibrated by these spectra.
AI.result: Detuning-dependent rovibrational Autler-Townes splitting is resolved in 13CO2, and the calibrated density-matrix model predicts transfer approaching 90%.
AI.conclusion: The scheme can exploit millisecond vibrational radiative lifetimes within the electronic ground state and extend to polar and nonpolar molecules with infrared-active vibrational modes.

title: Toward Long-Range Correlation Energies from Charge Fluctuations: Incorporating Exact Exchange into ACKS2$ω$
summary: Long-range electronic correlation can be represented in terms of coupled fluctuations of atomic charges and higher multipoles, motivating a density-response description beyond local dipolar polarization, particularly in low-dimensional, conducting, and small-gap systems where collective electronic fluctuations become important. We extend the frequency-dependent polarizable force field ACKS2$ω$ to electronic-structure references containing exact exchange by deriving both the static and additional frequency-dependent exchange contributions, with particular attention to HFsrPBE, which combines long-range Hartree--Fock exchange with short-range PBE exchange and correlation. Numerical validation of ACKS2$ω$ using dipole polarizabilities and $C_6$ dispersion coefficients for the 27 molecules of the TS27 set, with HF, PBE, B3LYP, and HFsrPBE as the underlying electronic-structure references, shows that including the exchange contributions and enriching the response basis improve agreement with the corresponding orbital-space linear-response calculations, although finite-response-basis errors remain molecule dependent. Long-range correlation energies evaluated through the adiabatic-connection fluctuation-dissipation theorem using the ACKS2$ω$ parameters reproduce the corresponding HFsrPBE orbital-space results for small test molecules when the response basis is made complete within the chosen orbital basis, while a local multipole decomposition resolves the finite-basis energies into monopole--monopole, mixed, dipole--dipole, and remaining higher-multipole contributions, providing a route to evaluating long-range correlation energies in terms of charge fluctuations within atom-condensed models.

AI.tldr: This work extends the frequency-dependent polarizable force field ACKS2ω to include exact-exchange references by deriving static and frequency-dependent exchange contributions, with focus on HFsrPBE, validated on polarizabilities and dispersion coefficients.
AI.motivation: Long-range electronic correlation involves coupled fluctuations of atomic charges and higher multipoles, which cannot be captured by local dipolar polarization alone. This is especially relevant in low-dimensional, conducting, and small-gap systems where collective electronic fluctuations matter, motivating a density-response description beyond local dipolar polarization.
AI.method: The authors extend the frequency-dependent polarizable force field ACKS2ω to electronic-structure references containing exact exchange, deriving both static and additional frequency-dependent exchange contributions. They give particular attention to HFsrPBE (long-range Hartree-Fock exchange combined with short-range PBE exchange and correlation). Validation uses dipole polarizabilities and C6 dispersion coefficients for the 27 molecules of the TS27 set, with HF, PBE, B3LYP, and HFsrPBE as underlying references. Long-range correlation energies are evaluated via the adiabatic-connection fluctuation-dissipation theorem using ACKS2ω parameters, and a local multipole decomposition resolves finite-basis energies.
AI.result: Including the exchange contributions and enriching the response basis improves agreement with corresponding orbital-space linear-response calculations, though finite-response-basis errors remain molecule dependent. For small test molecules, long-range correlation energies from ACKS2ω reproduce HFsrPBE orbital-space results when the response basis is made complete within the chosen orbital basis. The local multipole decomposition separates these energies into monopole--monopole, mixed, dipole--dipole, and remaining higher-multipole contributions.
AI.conclusion: Extending ACKS2ω with exchange contributions and an enriched response basis yields better consistency with orbital-space linear-response calculations. The multipole decomposition offers a route to evaluating long-range correlation energies in terms of charge fluctuations within atom-condensed models.

title: Orbital angular momentum in crystalline solids: non-equilibrium theory
summary: We develop a general operator theory of orbital angular momentum (OAM) in periodic solids that applies equally to equilibrium and coherently driven states. Employing the crystal momentum representation of Adams and Blount, we construct a periodic-solid OAM operator exactly corresponding to the symmetrized $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\mathbf v}$ observable, and show that it separates into local circulation (LC) and itinerant circulation (IC) sectors that are Hermitian and $U(1)$, and more generally $U(N)$, gauge covariant. In equilibrium, the LC and IC sectors reduce to the established modern theory of orbital magnetism; out of equilibrium, the same operator structure exposes new contributions generated by laser-written momentum-space textures and interband coherence. Applied to gapped graphene, we uncover a rich phenomenology of ultrafast non-equilibrium orbital angular momentum, including a quasi-stationary light-induced OAM. This latter finding, underpinned by a close connection between band-manifold phase texture and nonequilibrium OAM, points towards new possibilities for light control over OAM in solids as well as a potentially rich role for topological band structures in designed OAM materials.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a general operator theory of orbital angular momentum (OAM) in periodic solids, valid for both equilibrium and driven states, using the crystal momentum representation. The OAM operator splits into gauge-covariant local circulation (LC) and itinerant circulation (IC) sectors, reducing to the modern theory of orbital magnetism at equilibrium and exposing laser-induced nonequilibrium contributions otherwise. Applied to gapped graphene, it predicts a quasi-stationary light-induced OAM linked to band-manifold phase texture.
AI.motivation: Established theories of orbital magnetism in solids (e.g., the modern theory) address equilibrium OAM, but a unified operator framework that also captures coherently driven, nonequilibrium OAM is lacking. Such a framework is needed to understand light-induced OAM and its connection to band geometry/topology.
AI.method: Using the Adams-Blount crystal momentum representation, they construct a periodic-solid OAM operator exactly corresponding to the symmetrized r × v observable, and show it decomposes into LC and IC sectors that are Hermitian and U(1) (and U(N)) gauge covariant. They then apply this operator formalism to gapped graphene under coherent driving.
AI.result: At equilibrium the LC and IC sectors reduce to the established modern theory of orbital magnetism; out of equilibrium they reveal new contributions from laser-written momentum-space textures and interband coherence. In gapped graphene, this yields rich ultrafast nonequilibrium OAM phenomenology, including a quasi-stationary light-induced OAM rooted in band-manifold phase texture.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies equilibrium and nonequilibrium OAM in solids and suggests new routes for light control of OAM and for exploiting topological band structures in designed OAM materials.

title: RFBniCS: An open-source simulation framework for redox flow batteries
summary: We present RFBniCS, an open-source finite-element framework implemented in FEniCSx for simulating redox-flow-battery (RFB) half-cells. RFBniCS solves an established macro-homogeneous porous-electrode model accounting for strongly coupled electrolyte flow, multicomponent species transport, ionic and electronic charge conservation, and interfacial Faradaic charge transfer. Different from other open-access tools, RFBniCS can perform transient RFB half-cell simulations in one-, two-, and three-dimensional geometries while explicitly resolving the transport of both redox-active and supporting-electrolyte species. It also describes electrolyte flow through porous electrodes and, in the three-dimensional formulation, through adjacent flow channels. To verify the implementation, RFBniCS's predictions in parameter-limiting regimes are compared against other published implementations, with RFBniCS generally showing superior accuracy and speed. We further demonstrate RFBniCS's capabilities by a simulation of the transient response of the negative half-cell of a vanadium redox flow battery, with a moderately concentrated supporting electrolyte. In the current implementation, RFBniCS provides the computational basis for studying redox-flow-battery half-cells and can be extended to complex flow-field designs, alternative chemistries, full-cell coupling, detailed membrane transport, and additional multiphysics effects.

AI.tldr: RFBniCS is an open-source FEniCSx finite-element framework for transient 1D/2D/3D simulations of redox-flow-battery half-cells, resolving flow, multicomponent transport, charge conservation, and Faradaic kinetics, with verified accuracy and speed.
AI.motivation: Existing open-access RFB simulation tools generally cannot perform transient half-cell simulations across 1D, 2D, and 3D geometries while explicitly resolving both redox-active and supporting-electrolyte species transport, nor do they describe electrolyte flow through porous electrodes and adjacent flow channels in 3D.
AI.method: RFBniCS is implemented in FEniCSx and solves a macro-homogeneous porous-electrode model coupling electrolyte flow, multicomponent species transport, ionic and electronic charge conservation, and interfacial Faradaic charge transfer. Verification compares parameter-limiting regimes against published implementations.
AI.result: In parameter-limiting regimes, RFBniCS generally shows superior accuracy and speed compared with other published implementations. A demonstration simulates the transient response of a vanadium redox flow battery negative half-cell with a moderately concentrated supporting electrolyte.
AI.conclusion: RFBniCS provides a computational basis for studying RFB half-cells and is extensible to complex flow-field designs, alternative chemistries, full-cell coupling, detailed membrane transport, and additional multiphysics effects.

title: Near-infrared magnetic linear and non-reciprocal directional dichroism in the chiral antiferromagnet SmFe3(BO3)4
summary: We investigated the influence of antiferromagnetic (AFM) order on the near-infrared optical re- sponse of SmFe3(BO3)4 by polarization-resolved, magneto-optical spectroscopy. Below the Néel temperature, we observed pronounced magnetic linear dichroism at the 4f -4f transitions of Sm3+. By rotating the order parameter of the easy-plane AFM ground state using magnetic fields, we demonstrated the magnetic field control of linear dichroism, and deduced polarization selection rules. In addition, we detected non-reciprocal directional dichroism for several 4f -4f transitions. The non-reciprocal absorption appears in the symmetry-allowed toroidal geometry when the in- plane magnetic field is normal to one of the two-fold rotation axes. These results indicate a strong interference between electric- and magnetic-dipole excitations for transitions showing non-reciprocal absorption. The observed optical anisotropies provide a promising path to detect the in-plane orien- tation of the AFM order, enabling imaging and time-resolved studies of the AFM order parameter in rare-earth ferroborates.

AI.tldr: Polarization-resolved magneto-optical spectroscopy on SmFe3(BO3)4 reveals pronounced magnetic linear dichroism and non-reciprocal directional dichroism at Sm3+ 4f-4f transitions below the Néel temperature, driven by antiferromagnetic order.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnetic (AFM) order is difficult to detect and manipulate optically because of its lack of net magnetization. The authors aim to exploit the coupling between the AFM order parameter and optical excitations of Sm3+ 4f electrons to enable detection and control of the AFM state in rare-earth ferroborates.
AI.method: Polarization-resolved, magneto-optical spectroscopy of SmFe3(BO3)4 in the near-infrared, focusing on the 4f-4f transitions of Sm3+. The AFM order parameter (easy-plane ground state) is rotated with applied magnetic fields, and polarization selection rules are deduced from the resulting linear dichroism. Non-reciprocal directional dichroism is examined in the symmetry-allowed toroidal geometry with an in-plane magnetic field normal to a two-fold rotation axis.
AI.result: Below the Néel temperature, pronounced magnetic linear dichroism appears at the Sm3+ 4f-4f transitions. The linear dichroism is controllable by magnetic field through rotation of the AFM order parameter. Non-reciprocal directional dichroism is detected for several 4f-4f transitions, appearing in the symmetry-allowed toroidal geometry when the in-plane field is normal to a two-fold rotation axis. These observations indicate strong interference between electric- and magnetic-dipole excitations for the transitions showing non-reciprocal absorption.
AI.conclusion: The observed optical anisotropies provide a promising route to detect the in-plane orientation of AFM order, enabling imaging and time-resolved studies of the AFM order parameter in rare-earth ferroborates.

title: The Ericson Transition in Time-Reversal Invariant Systems: Symplectically Invariant Hamiltonians
summary: We investigate the distributions of off-diagonal scattering matrix elements and cross-sections in the Ericson regime for time-reversal invariant systems with odd spin. Within the universal Heidelberg approach we prove that Gaussian and exponential behavior is found as the leading-order term of an asymptotic expansion of the aforementioned distributions. Furthermore, the subleading-order term is derived and compared with numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: Using the universal Heidelberg approach, the authors prove that off-diagonal scattering matrix elements and cross-sections in the Ericson regime (time-reversal invariant, odd-spin systems) follow Gaussian and exponential distributions as leading-order asymptotic terms, and they derive the subleading-order corrections, validating them against numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: The statistical distributions of scattering observables in the Ericson (overlapping-resonance) regime are central to quantum chaotic scattering, but their precise asymptotic form—particularly beyond leading order—needed rigorous treatment for the specific symmetry class of time-reversal invariant systems with odd spin.
AI.method: Analytical derivation within the universal Heidelberg approach, combining random-matrix-theoretic ensemble averaging with an asymptotic expansion of the off-diagonal scattering matrix element and cross-section distributions; results benchmarked against numerical simulations.
AI.result: Gaussian and exponential distributions emerge as the leading-order asymptotic terms for the off-diagonal S-matrix elements and cross-sections, respectively; the subleading-order term is explicitly derived and shows good agreement with numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian/exponential law in the Ericson regime is confirmed as a rigorous asymptotic result for odd-spin, time-reversal invariant systems, and the inclusion of subleading corrections refines the description of finite-size or finite-parameter deviations.

title: Determination of van der Waals thin film thickness via characteristic X-ray photon yield
summary: Characteristic X ray generation is essential for producing X ray sources and for investigating light matter interactions. Here, we demonstrate that characteristic X ray generation can also be employed to determine the thickness of van der Waals thin films in a non destructive manner. Specifically, we establish a sixth order polynomial model that relates film thickness to the characteristic X ray yield. The model can both predict the X ray yield of graphite films at arbitrary thicknesses and infer the film thickness from a corresponding characteristic X ray yield. We validate the model by comparing its predicted X ray yields for graphite films with those obtained from Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we experimentally validated the reliability and feasibility of the proposed method for extracting graphite film thickness via X ray photon yield characterization. Our results provide a non destructive approach for determining the thickness of van der Waals thin films.

AI.tldr: A sixth-order polynomial links characteristic X-ray yield to film thickness, allowing non-destructive thickness determination of van der Waals (graphite) thin films; validated by Monte Carlo simulations and experiments.
AI.motivation: Determining the thickness of van der Waals thin films typically requires destructive or complex methods; a non-destructive, accessible alternative is desirable. Characteristic X-ray generation, well established for X-ray sources and light-matter interaction studies, is repurposed here as a thickness metrology tool.
AI.method: A sixth-order polynomial model is established relating film thickness to characteristic X-ray yield. The model predicts X-ray yield for graphite films at arbitrary thicknesses and inversely infers film thickness from a measured characteristic X-ray yield. Validation combines Monte Carlo simulations of X-ray yields for graphite films with experimental characterization of X-ray photon yield.
AI.result: Model-predicted X-ray yields for graphite films agree with Monte Carlo simulations. Experimental measurements confirm the reliability and feasibility of extracting graphite film thickness from characteristic X-ray photon yield.
AI.conclusion: Characteristic X-ray generation enables a non-destructive approach for determining the thickness of van der Waals thin films, demonstrated on graphite films via a sixth-order polynomial thickness–yield relation.

title: Strongly coupled ultracompressed self-cavity plasmon polaritons at millikelvin temperatures
summary: Van der Waals heterostructures exhibit self-cavity resonances from sub-terahertz to terahertz frequencies and thus offer an attractive route toward realizing cavity-modified phases of matter. Spectroscopy of such systems calls for high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures, which is extremely challenging with existing methods. Here we demonstrate a new platform for realizing and probing such systems. Superconducting layers define self-cavity structures with electromagnetic volume compression of order $10^7$. With an integrated graphene layer, we observe underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons at frequencies as low as 0.04 THz and which exhibit avoided crossings with cavity modes. To measure such spectra, we deploy a millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer based on a superconducting circuit. This work paves the way for simultaneous spectroscopy and transport measurements of cavity-matter hybrid systems at millikelvin temperatures.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer using superconducting self-cavity structures with graphene, enabling observation of underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons down to 0.04 THz and avoided crossings with cavity modes.
AI.motivation: Van der Waals heterostructures show self-cavity resonances from sub-THz to THz frequencies, offering a route to cavity-modified phases of matter. However, spectroscopy of these systems requires high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures, which is extremely challenging with existing methods.
AI.method: The authors create superconducting-layer-defined self-cavity structures with electromagnetic volume compression of order 10^7 and integrate a graphene layer. They deploy a millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer based on a superconducting circuit to measure the spectra.
AI.result: Underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons are observed at frequencies as low as 0.04 THz, exhibiting avoided crossings with cavity modes.
AI.conclusion: This work paves the way for simultaneous spectroscopy and transport measurements of cavity-matter hybrid systems at millikelvin temperatures.

title: SupraTITO: Transferable Generative Molecular Dynamics for Supramolecular Systems
summary: Peptide sequence governs both the structures formed through supramolecular assembly and the dynamics by which they emerge, but predicting either requires resolving slow collective processes among many interacting molecules. Molecular dynamics (MD) provides microscopic insight into these processes, yet the long timescales of assembly and the vast peptide sequence space make systematic exploration computationally demanding. We introduce SupraTITO, a transferable generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) framework for supramolecular systems, demonstrated through peptide self-assembly. SupraTITO learns transferable implicit transfer operators (TITO) conditioned on peptide sequence, molecular topology, and periodic geometry, allowing configurations to be propagated over physical intervals much longer than an MD integration step. On a comprehensive dipeptide benchmark, SupraTITO generalizes to held-out sequences and reproduces sequence-dependent structures and dynamics while maintaining molecular integrity over long rollouts. Compared with direct ensemble prediction trained on the same trajectory data, SupraTITO more accurately reproduces assembly structures while also resolving their temporal evolution. The learned dynamics generalize across peptide concentrations, including dilute conditions not represented during training. These results extend transferable GenMD to collective dynamics in periodic supramolecular systems and provide a foundation for modeling related processes beyond peptide assembly.

AI.tldr: SupraTITO is a transferable generative molecular dynamics framework that learns sequence-, topology-, and geometry-conditioned implicit transfer operators to propagate peptide self-assembly over long timescales, generalizing to held-out sequences and unseen concentrations.
AI.motivation: Peptide sequence determines both the supramolecular structures formed during assembly and the dynamics of their emergence, but predicting either requires resolving slow collective processes among many interacting molecules. MD offers microscopic insight but is computationally prohibitive due to long assembly timescales and the vast sequence space. There is a need for a transferable framework that captures collective assembly dynamics efficiently.
AI.method: The authors introduce SupraTITO, a transferable generative MD (GenMD) framework for supramolecular systems. It learns transferable implicit transfer operators (TITO) conditioned on peptide sequence, molecular topology, and periodic geometry, enabling configuration propagation over physical intervals far longer than a single MD integration step. It is demonstrated on peptide self-assembly and benchmarked on a comprehensive dipeptide dataset.
AI.result: On the dipeptide benchmark, SupraTITO generalizes to held-out sequences and reproduces sequence-dependent structures and dynamics while preserving molecular integrity over long rollouts. Compared with direct ensemble prediction trained on the same trajectory data, it more accurately reproduces assembly structures and resolves their temporal evolution. Learned dynamics also generalize across peptide concentrations, including dilute conditions absent from training.
AI.conclusion: SupraTITO extends transferable GenMD to collective dynamics in periodic supramolecular systems and provides a foundation for modeling related processes beyond peptide assembly.

title: Reference-free certification of machine-learning interatomic potentials
summary: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials now reach held-out energy and force errors so small that they no longer predict how a model behaves in simulation. Here we show that a potential can be graded without any reference calculation, against properties the exact Born-Oppenheimer surface satisfies by mathematical or physical necessity. We organise these properties into four families, symmetry and invariance, self-consistency and integrability, statistical-mechanical equilibrium and regularity, and turn them into fourteen inexpensive probes, each certifying against a target that is exact and independent of chemistry and reference method. Every probe therefore returns an absolute, architecture-comparable score from the energies, forces and stresses a potential already exposes, and reveals failures a fixed test set cannot. Applied to 64 pretrained potentials, the suite resolves two orders of magnitude of certified quality at comparable reported accuracy, and flags a fine-tuned potential whose reference errors improve while its surface degrades until molecular dynamics fails. An interactive leaderboard of all 64 models is available at https://jhaens.github.io/pescert-bench.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a reference-free grading scheme for machine-learning interatomic potentials, based on exact mathematical/physical properties of the Born-Oppenheimer surface, organized into four families and fourteen probes, and demonstrate it on 64 pretrained models.
AI.motivation: Universal ML interatomic potentials now achieve held-out energy and force errors so small that these errors no longer predict how a model behaves in simulation. Existing evaluation relies on fixed reference test sets, which cannot expose such behavioral failures or distinguish models of comparable reported accuracy.
AI.method: The method grades a potential without any reference calculation, using properties the exact Born-Oppenheimer surface satisfies by mathematical or physical necessity. These properties are organized into four families: symmetry and invariance; self-consistency and integrability; statistical-mechanical equilibrium and regularity. They are turned into fourteen inexpensive probes, each certifying against a target that is exact and independent of chemistry and reference method. Each probe yields an absolute, architecture-comparable score computed from the energies, forces and stresses a potential already exposes.
AI.result: Applied to 64 pretrained potentials, the probe suite resolves two orders of magnitude of certified quality at comparable reported accuracy. It also flags a fine-tuned potential whose reference errors improve while its surface degrades until molecular dynamics fails. An interactive leaderboard of all 64 models is provided at https://jhaens.github.io/pescert-bench.
AI.conclusion: Reference-free, exact-certificate probes provide an absolute and architecture-comparable measure of potential quality, revealing failures invisible to fixed test sets and enabling ranking of models that appear equally accurate by conventional metrics.

title: Mechanism of Incommensurate Magnetic Order in $\mathrm{BaCo_2(AsO_4)_2}$: Interplay of Frustrated Further-Neighbor Exchanges and Bond-Directional Anisotropy
summary: The microscopic mechanism governing the zero-field incommensurate magnetic order in the honeycomb cobaltate $\mathrm{BaCo}_2(\mathrm{AsO}_4)_2$ remains a significant unresolved problem, particularly concerning the relative contributions of bond-directional Kitaev-type interactions and exchange frustration. This study investigates an extended $J_1\text{--}K\text{--}Γ\text{--}Γ'\text{--}J_2\text{--}J_3$ model, which incorporates XXZ-type exchange anisotropies on the honeycomb lattice. Nearest-neighbor parameters are constrained by ab initio electronic structure calculations. Instead, this phase arises naturally from the synergistic interplay between exchange frustration, driven by further-neighbor couplings ($J_2, J_3$), and intermediate off-diagonal bond anisotropies ($Γ, Γ'$). In the quantum regime, we elucidate the competition between this incommensurate manifold and an out-of-plane ferromagnetic ($\mathrm{FM}_z$) phase, which is selectively stabilized via a quantum order-by-disorder mechanism. Our findings reconcile conflicting interpretations of the magnetic interactions in $\mathrm{BaCo}_2(\mathrm{AsO}_4)_2$ and establish the microscopic origin and stability range of its incommensurate ground state.

title: CTMRG as a tensor-network message-passing algorithm
summary: We formulate the corner transfer matrix equations, and the corner transfer matrix renormalization group built on them, as a set of local equations on general planar graphs. These equations depend only on the local subgraphs of the planar graph and are glued together consistently to describe the whole graph. Solving them yields message tensors and corner matrices, which can be used to construct an MPS environment for any connected subgraph. We test the proposed equations on the ferromagnetic Ising model, on a variety of infinite lattices (including hyperbolic ones) and on finite graphs, and find systematic improvement over belief propagation.

AI.motivation: Existing CTMRG and related tensor-network methods are typically tied to specific lattice geometries, limiting their applicability to general planar graphs such as hyperbolic or irregular lattices. There is a need for a geometry-independent, local formulation that can be assembled consistently on arbitrary planar graphs.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the corner transfer matrix equations and the corner transfer matrix renormalization group as a set of local equations defined on general planar graphs. These equations depend only on local subgraphs and are glued together consistently. Solving them produces message tensors and corner matrices, which are then used to construct a matrix product state (MPS) environment for any connected subgraph.

title: HVPE Homoepitaxy of $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$: High-Temperature Growth and Orientation-Dependent Surface Evolution
summary: In this work, we systematically investigate homoepitaxial $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ growth by halide vapor phase epitaxy (HVPE) on (010), (001), and ($\bar{2}$01) native substrates over a broad growth parameter space, extending the growth temperature as high as 1150 $^\circ$C. The growth kinetics exhibit strong dependence on precursor supply, temperature, reactor pressure, and Ga-source-to-substrate distance. Increasing the HCl flow from 80 to 300 sccm enhances the growth rate by up to seven-fold, while increasing the temperature from 1050 to 1150 $^\circ$C nearly doubles the deposition rate. At 1150 $^\circ$C, atmospheric-pressure growth yields rates more than 2.5 times higher than those at 100 Torr, while reducing the O$_2$ flow to 5 sccm further increases the growth rate to 14.3 $μ$m/h, producing films up to 42.9 $μ$m thick in 3 h. Notably, phase-pure homoepitaxial layers with good crystalline quality are obtained across all three orientations, with low rocking-curve full width at half maximum (FWHM) values of 63.4, 66.6, and 42.8 arcsec for the (010), (001), and ($\bar{2}$01) epilayers, respectively. The surface morphology exhibits a pronounced crystallographic dependence and evolves strongly with the HVPE growth conditions. In particular, the ($\bar{2}$01) surface develops well-defined step-and-terrace morphology with local RMS roughness as low as 0.17 nm. These results extend $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ HVPE homoepitaxy into a higher-temperature regime and demonstrate a broad process window for high-rate growth of thick, high-quality epilayers with strongly orientation-dependent surface evolution.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of homoepitaxial β-Ga₂O₃ HVPE on (010), (001), and (2̄01) substrates up to 1150 °C, showing strong orientation-dependent growth kinetics and enabling high-rate growth of thick, high-quality, phase-pure epilayers with smooth step-and-terrace surfaces.
AI.motivation: β-Ga₂O₃ is an important ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor, but high-rate growth of thick, high-quality homoepitaxial layers requires a broader understanding of HVPE growth kinetics and how they depend on orientation and process parameters. Extending growth into a higher-temperature regime and mapping the process window are needed to enable thick device-grade epilayers.

title: Algebraic Relaxation of Strong-to-Weak Symmetry-Breaking Order via Charge-Sector Broadening
summary: Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) is a distinctive phenomenon of mixed quantum states, characterized by nonlinear long-range order associated with strong symmetry. In realistic open quantum systems, however, strong symmetry is macroscopically fragile and can be explicitly reduced to weak symmetry through local charge exchange with the environment. In this paper, we investigate how the SW-SSB order decays under such strong-symmetry-breaking Liouvillian dynamics. For discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a local symmetry-breaking perturbation drives an exponential decay of the Rényi-1 long-range correlator, revealing the fragility of discrete SW-SSB order. By contrast, for continuous $U(1)$ symmetry, local charge exchange broadens the distribution over symmetry-charge sectors and leads to parametrically slower algebraic relaxation. We establish a rigorous algebraic lower bound on the connected Rényi-1 long-range correlation, demonstrating the robustness of this slow relaxation. In the thermodynamic limit, we further uncover a two-stage dynamical scaling: $\tilde{R}_1\sim t^{-1}$ at early times and $\tilde{R}_1\sim t^{-1/z}$ at long times, with $z$ set by the underlying hydrodynamic dynamics. As a numerical verification, we consider fermionic chains with $z=2$ and $z=4$, which are excellent agreement with the theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) order decays under Liouvillian dynamics that explicitly break strong symmetry via local charge exchange with the environment.
AI.motivation: SW-SSB is a hallmark of mixed quantum states, but realistic open systems make strong symmetry macroscopically fragile as it can be explicitly reduced to weak symmetry through local coupling to the environment. The fate of SW-SSB order under such strong-symmetry-breaking Liouvillian dynamics was previously unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze the decay of the Rényi-1 long-range correlator under local symmetry-breaking Liouvillian perturbations. They treat discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry and continuous $U(1)$ symmetry separately, deriving a rigorous algebraic lower bound on the connected Rényi-1 long-range correlation for the $U(1)$ case. They further perform numerical verification using fermionic chains with dynamical exponents $z=2$ and $z=4$.
AI.result: For discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a local symmetry-breaking perturbation drives exponential decay of the Rényi-1 long-range correlator, showing fragility of discrete SW-SSB order. For continuous $U(1)$ symmetry, local charge exchange broadens the distribution over symmetry-charge sectors and yields parametrically slower algebraic relaxation, with a rigorous algebraic lower bound confirming its robustness. In the thermodynamic limit, a two-stage dynamical scaling emerges: $\tilde{R}_1\sim t^{-1}$ at early times and $\tilde{R}_1\sim t^{-1/z}$ at long times, where $z$ is set by the underlying hydrodynamic dynamics. Numerical results for fermionic chains with $z=2$ and $z=4$ agree excellently with the theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Strong-symmetry-breaking Liouvillian dynamics destroy discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ SW-SSB exponentially but only induce slow algebraic relaxation for continuous $U(1)$ SW-SSB, with a two-stage dynamical scaling governed by hydrodynamic exponents. This reveals a sharp contrast between discrete and continuous SW-SSB robustness in open quantum systems.

title: Deciphering the internal conversion and triplet formation in thymine via time-resolved multi-center X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
summary: The photostability of DNA nucleobases relies on ultrafast nonradiative relaxation following ultraviolet excitation. In thymine, the competition between internal conversion (IC) and intersystem crossing (ISC) determines the balance between ultrafast energy dissipation and potentially long-lived photochemistry. However, the precise molecular mechanisms linking early singlet-state electronic and structural evolution to the formation of long-lived triplet dark states remain unresolved. Here, we investigate the gas-phase photodynamics of thymine using time-resolved multi-center X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (tr-mc-XPS) supported by state-of-the-art ab initio quantum calculations. By simultaneously probing multiple carbon 1s core levels, we track site-specific electronic and nuclear dynamics. We discover that the long-lived dark state is not initially a pure triplet; rather, it exists as a mixture of singlet and triplet states for the first 240 ps before transitioning fully to the $^3ππ^*$ state. On the femtosecond timescale, we resolve atom-specific vibrational coherence at $\sim$730 cm$^{-1}$ (a ring-breathing mode with a period of 46 fs) that survives the initial $^1ππ^*$ to $^1nπ^*$ IC. Furthermore, we identify a critical dual role for the methyl group (C9H$_3$). During singlet relaxation, the methyl group acts as an inertia spectator, and its mass hinders direct internal conversion to the ground state. Upon $^3ππ^*$ state formation, however, state-dependent hyperconjugation couples the methyl group to the pyrimidine ring, turning it into a highly sensitive electronic reporter of ISC. These findings establish tr-mc-XPS as a powerful approach for disentangling the complex, multi-timescale photodynamics governing nucleobase stability.

AI.tldr: Time-resolved multi-center X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (tr-mc-XPS) combined with ab initio calculations resolves the gas-phase photodynamics of thymine, revealing that the long-lived dark state is a singlet–triplet mixture for the first 240 ps, atom-specific vibrational coherence at ~730 cm⁻¹, and a dual spectator/reporter role of the methyl group.
AI.motivation: The photostability of DNA nucleobases depends on ultrafast nonradiative relaxation after UV excitation. In thymine, the competition between internal conversion (IC) and intersystem crossing (ISC) governs the balance between fast energy dissipation and long-lived photochemistry, but the molecular mechanisms connecting early singlet-state electronic and structural evolution to the formation of long-lived triplet dark states remain unresolved.
AI.method: Gas-phase thymine is studied with time-resolved multi-center X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (tr-mc-XPS), supported by state-of-the-art ab initio quantum calculations. Multiple carbon 1s core levels are probed simultaneously to track site-specific electronic and nuclear dynamics.

Atom-specific vibrational coherence at ~730 cm⁻¹ (a ring-breathing mode with a 46 fs period) is resolved on the femtosecond timescale and survives the initial ¹ππ* → ¹nπ* IC. The methyl group (C9H₃) plays a dual role: during singlet relaxation it acts as an inertia spectator whose mass hinders direct IC to the ground state, whereas upon ³ππ* formation state-dependent hyperconjugation couples it to the pyrimidine ring, making it a sensitive electronic reporter of ISC.
AI.conclusion: tr-mc-XPS is established as a powerful approach for disentangling the complex, multi-timescale photodynamics that govern nucleobase stability, and it reveals that the thymine dark state is a mixed singlet–triplet species before reaching the pure ³ππ* state.

title: Long-Range Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Defect Energetics in SrTiO$_3$
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have advanced rapidly in recent years, yet the majority of models remain semilocal in nature and neglect long-range electrostatic interactions. A growing number of long-range models have emerged to address this limitation, but systematic benchmarks comparing their performance on physically realistic systems remain scarce. In this work, we assess three long-range MLIPs -- MACE-POLAR, MACE-LES, and LOREM, against a short-range baseline MACE model, on their ability to capture long-range Coulombic interactions, progressing from idealised synthetic point-charge systems to first-principles data on realistic crystal structures. This progression allows us to isolate model's capability to learn electrostatic interactions from the many competing energy contributions, such as dielectric screening and exchange-correlation, that are present in DFT total energies. As a physically motivated benchmark system, we focus on strontium titanate SrTiO$_3$ with Sr--O Schottky vacancy pairs, a material in which long-range charge interactions play a central role and which serves as a natural stepping stone towards the study of charged polarons and other electronic and optical properties. Building on this benchmark, we further examine oxygen vacancy migration in the presence of the Sr--O Schottky pair, using climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations and molecular dynamics to obtain activation barriers as a function of the vacancy pair separation, providing further extrapolation test of each model's ability to capture the electrostatic effects that govern defect transport.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks three long-range MLIPs (MACE-POLAR, MACE-LES, LOREM) against a short-range MACE baseline, progressing from synthetic point charges to DFT data on SrTiO$_3$ with Sr–O Schottky vacancy pairs, and further testing oxygen vacancy migration barriers versus pair separation via CI-NEB and MD.
AI.motivation: Most MLIPs are semilocal and neglect long-range electrostatic interactions; although long-range models have emerged, systematic benchmarks on physically realistic systems are scarce. A rigorous benchmark is needed to isolate a model's ability to learn electrostatics from competing contributions such as dielectric screening and exchange-correlation present in DFT total energies.
AI.method: Assess three long-range MLIPs (MACE-POLAR, MACE-LES, LOREM) against a short-range MACE baseline. Use a progressive benchmark: idealised synthetic point-charge systems, then first-principles data on realistic crystal structures. Focus on SrTiO$_3$ with Sr–O Schottky vacancy pairs as the physically motivated system. Extend the benchmark to oxygen vacancy migration in the presence of the Schottky pair, using climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) to obtain activation barriers as a function of vacancy pair separation.
AI.result: The progressive design allows isolation of each model's capability to learn electrostatic interactions from competing energy contributions (dielectric screening, exchange-correlation) in DFT total energies. Activation barriers for oxygen vacancy migration are obtained as a function of Sr–O Schottky pair separation, providing an extrapolation test of each model's ability to capture the electrostatic effects governing defect transport.
AI.conclusion: Long-range MLIPs are evaluated on their ability to capture long-range Coulombic interactions, from synthetic point charges to DFT data on realistic crystals. SrTiO$_3$ with Sr–O Schottky vacancy pairs serves as a stepping stone toward studying charged polarons and other electronic and optical properties, while the vacancy-migration benchmark tests extrapolative capture of electrostatics that govern defect transport.

title: The half-filled optical Su-Schrieffer-Heeger-Hubbard model with uniaxial strain
summary: Strain offers a direct route to control electronic phases by altering bond lengths, hopping amplitudes, and lattice symmetries. These aspects make electron-phonon (e-ph) coupled systems a natural setting to study strain-induced effects. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) Hamiltonian describes the coupling between itinerant electrons and lattice degrees of freedom that modulate hopping and is thus expected to be strongly affected by strain fields. At half-filling and on a bipartite lattice, the SSH interactions drive dominant bond-order-wave (BOW) correlations at low- temperature in which short bonds with high kinetic energy alternate with long bonds with low kinetic energy along four possible patterns. We model uniaxial strain through anisotropic hopping, which breaks the $90^\circ$ rotational symmetry and reduces the BOW phase degeneracy to two. We also include an on-site Hubbard U that promotes antiferromagnetic correlations that are also (weakly) driven by the SSH interaction itself. We map out the half-filled phase diagram in the plane of the e-ph and Hubbard couplings, and determine the critical temperature of BOW formation. Using analytic continuation, we also evaluate the spectral function and demonstrate directionally dependent gap formation in the BOW phase

AI.tldr: Anisotropic hopping modeling uniaxial strain reduces the fourfold degenerate bond-order-wave (BOW) phase of the half-filled Su-Schrieffer-Heeger-Hubbard model to twofold degeneracy, and the half-filled phase diagram and BOW critical temperature are mapped as functions of electron-phonon and Hubbard couplings.
AI.motivation: Strain controls electronic phases by modifying bond lengths, hopping amplitudes, and lattice symmetries, making electron-phonon coupled systems a natural platform for strain-induced effects. The SSH Hamiltonian, which couples itinerant electrons to hopping-modulating lattice degrees of freedom, is expected to be strongly affected by strain fields, yet the interplay of strain, SSH bond-order correlations, and Hubbard antiferromagnetic correlations remains to be characterized.
AI.method: Uniaxial strain is modeled via anisotropic hopping, which breaks 90-degree rotational symmetry and reduces the BOW phase degeneracy from four patterns to two. An on-site Hubbard U is included to capture antiferromagnetic correlations, which are also weakly promoted by the SSH interaction. The half-filled phase diagram is mapped in the plane of electron-phonon and Hubbard couplings, the BOW critical temperature is determined, and the spectral function is evaluated via analytic continuation.
AI.result: Strain reduces the BOW degeneracy from four to two. A half-filled phase diagram is obtained in the electron-phonon versus Hubbard coupling plane, the critical temperature of BOW formation is determined, and the spectral function reveals directionally dependent gap formation in the BOW phase.
AI.conclusion: Strain via anisotropic hopping lifts part of the BOW degeneracy and, together with Hubbard interactions, governs the competition between bond-order-wave and antiferromagnetic correlations at half filling, producing an anisotropic gap in the BOW phase.

title: Thermal entanglement transitions from strong $\textrm{SU}(2)$ symmetry
summary: We study mixed-state entanglement in Gibbs states with strong $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ symmetry, focusing on locally interacting spin systems with ferromagnetic interactions. Our main result is to show that finite-temperature ordering transitions are associated with entanglement transitions, and therefore the steady state of strongly symmetric Lindbladians can exhibit entanglement transitions. While in the paramagnetic phase it is known that the distillable entanglement and logarithmic entanglement negativity between two halves of a large system grow logarithmically with the square root of the number of spins, we show that in ferromagnetic phases these quantities grow parametrically faster with system size. To arrive at this result we first establish relations between these mixed-state entanglement measures and spin correlations in states that are singlets under global $\rm{SU}(2)$ symmetry transformations. We then introduce a semiclassical theory for $\rm{SU}(2)$ singlet thermal states. While the global singlet constraint generally enters this theory as a complicated function of the full semiclassical spin configuration, we show that in large $S$ limit it simplifies drastically to a Gaussian suppression of total magnetization in disordered phases as well as in ordered phases in the vicinity of continuous thermal phase transitions. This leads us to a field theory describing spin correlations in the singlet sector. Using this we determine the behavior of various probes of mixed-state entanglement at low and at high temperatures, supporting our analytical results using numerical Monte Carlo simulations of a three-dimensional lattice realization of our semiclassical theory. We also use exact numerics in one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ systems to confirm our predictions for the scaling of mixed-state entanglement with correlation length and system size in the paramagnetic phase.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that finite-temperature ordering transitions in strongly SU(2)-symmetric ferromagnetic spin systems coincide with entanglement transitions, with ferromagnetic phases showing parametrically faster growth of distillable entanglement and logarithmic negativity than the paramagnetic phase.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether mixed-state entanglement can exhibit phase transitions, and specifically whether finite-temperature ordering transitions correspond to entanglement transitions, particularly in strongly symmetric Lindbladians whose steady states are Gibbs states. Motivated by the need to characterize entanglement behavior across paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases beyond the known logarithmic (square-root-of-N) scaling.
AI.method: Establishes relations between mixed-state entanglement measures (distillable entanglement, logarithmic negativity) and spin correlations in global SU(2) singlet states; introduces a semiclassical theory for SU(2) singlet thermal states, showing the singlet constraint simplifies in the large-S limit to a Gaussian suppression of total magnetization (in disordered phases and near continuous transitions); derives a field theory for spin correlations in the singlet sector; supports with Monte Carlo simulations of a 3D lattice and exact numerics in 1D spin-1/2 systems.
AI.result: Finite-temperature ordering transitions are associated with entanglement transitions. In the paramagnetic phase, distillable entanglement and logarithmic negativity between two halves grow logarithmically with the square root of the number of spins; in ferromagnetic phases these quantities grow parametrically faster with system size. Numerical simulations (3D Monte Carlo, 1D exact) confirm predictions for scaling with correlation length and system size in the paramagnetic phase.
AI.conclusion: Steady states of strongly symmetric Lindbladians can exhibit entanglement transitions. The semiclassical framework links thermodynamic ordering to entanglement scaling, showing entanglement measures grow faster in ordered (ferromagnetic) phases than in disordered phases.

title: Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors for Mechanistic Ion Transport Pathways from Static Crystal Structures
summary: Ion transport controls the macroscopic performance of solid electrolytes, battery electrodes, ion-selective membranes, electrolysis ceramics, mixed conductors, porous sorbents, and biological channels. In each case, ion transport is determined by structural characteristics, namely the available diffusion pathways and the specific bottleneck atoms that limit the ionic jumps. These are intrinsic properties of the crystalline framework, whereas temperature, carrier concentration, and correlated motion govern the transport rate. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) resolves the mechanism directly but is too costly for materials screening, and most surrogate models give only a single transport number. Here we present a calibration-free method for determining the mechanism, based on Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors (TSPD). TSPD obtains the transport mechanism from a single static structure in seconds. It constructs a periodic migration network whose edge barriers are computed from physics-based energetics. We then analyze the barrier-threshold topology of this network and the spectrum of its barrier-weighted graph Laplacian. To establish its validity for computational solid-state ionics, we test TSPD against AIMD ion densities and neutron diffraction data for eight materials, including cathodes and solid electrolytes, whose transport ranges from one- to three-dimensional. TSPD reproduces the established mechanism in every case and correctly identifies structures in which geometric openness does not imply viable ion percolation. The method is most informative for pathway-limited, direction-dependent transport, and it complements full dynamical simulations for strongly cooperative or nearly isotropic transport.

AI.tldr: TSPD is a calibration-free, seconds-fast descriptor that predicts solid-state ion transport mechanisms from a single static structure, validated against AIMD and neutron diffraction across eight materials.
AI.motivation: Ion transport governs the performance of solid electrolytes, electrodes, membranes, ceramics, and biological channels. The transport mechanism is set by intrinsic structural features—available diffusion pathways and bottleneck atoms—but AIMD, while mechanistically direct, is too expensive for materials screening, and most surrogate models return only a single aggregate transport number rather than the mechanism.
AI.method: Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors (TSPD): from one static structure, a periodic migration network is built with edge barriers derived from physics-based energetics; the barrier-threshold topology of the network and the spectrum of its barrier-weighted graph Laplacian are then analyzed to extract the transport mechanism.
AI.result: Tested against AIMD ion densities and neutron diffraction data for eight materials (cathodes and solid electrolytes) spanning 1D to 3D transport, TSPD reproduces the established mechanism in every case and correctly identifies structures where geometric openness does not imply viable ion percolation.
AI.conclusion: TSPD provides a calibration-free, computationally cheap route to mechanistic ion-transport prediction, is most informative for pathway-limited, direction-dependent transport, and complements full dynamical simulations for strongly cooperative or nearly isotropic transport.

title: How Superradiance Survives Molecular Noise inside Virus Capsids
summary: Excited organic dyes chemically bound to an icosahedral virus shell can spontaneously synchronize and emit a superradiant burst of light. The mechanism that allows it to occur at room temperature, despite collisional dephasing and inhomogeneous broadening, is not understood. Few other known low-dimensional condensed matter systems exhibit room-temperature superradiance (SR). In the fluctuation-prone environment of molecular-based systems, electron--vibrational coupling has been proposed to play a central role. Here, we addressed experimentally the existence of underdamped virus capsid phonon-like modes and theoretically their involvement in the transition from uncorrelated to cooperative emission. We find that SR-active dye-labeled capsids exhibit underdamped low-frequency oscillations that modulate the dye excited-state response, and modeling shows how such capsid motion can promote the collective polarization required for superradiant emission.

The authors experimentally identify underdamped low-frequency virus capsid phonon-like modes that modulate the dye excited-state response, and modeling shows these motions can promote the collective polarization required for superradiant emission.

In fluctuation-prone molecular systems subject to collisional dephasing and inhomogeneous broadening, the mechanism enabling room-temperature SR remains unexplained. Electron-vibrational coupling has been proposed as central, motivating an investigation of capsid vibrational modes and their role in the transition from uncorrelated to cooperative emission.

AI.result: SR-active dye-labeled capsids exhibit underdamped low-frequency oscillations that modulate the dye excited-state response. Modeling demonstrates how this capsid motion can promote the collective polarization necessary for superradiant emission.
AI.conclusion: Coupling between dye excited states and underdamped capsid vibrational modes provides a plausible mechanism for room-temperature superradiance, linking electron-vibrational coupling to cooperative emission in molecular-based systems.

title: Numerical integration of intracule pair densities with optimized multicenter grids
summary: Intracule pair densities provide insight into electron correlation, but their routine analysis in extended systems is limited by the cost of numerical integration and the restriction of analytical methods to Gaussian basis functions. We present an efficient multicenter integration scheme for intracule densities and their moments. By adapting the topological fuzzy Voronoi cell formalism, we partition intracule space around interatomic displacement vectors, concentrating quadrature points near secondary density maxima that standard single-center grids poorly resolve. Benchmarks on linear alkanes show improved convergence with increasing molecular size, achieving relative errors below 0.02% in electron-electron repulsion energies with fewer quadrature points than single-center methods. The partitioning also enables the decomposition of global two-electron properties into spatial contributions associated with short- and long-range electron-pair separations. Coupling the multicenter grid with kernel density estimation reconstructs smooth radial intracule distributions at large interelectronic distances without the dense angular grids required by conventional surface integration. Validation on the S22 dataset supports the reliability of the method across diverse molecular systems. These developments facilitate intracule analysis in polyatomic systems and the investigation of electron correlation and dispersion interactions.

It improves convergence, enables spatial decomposition of two-electron properties, and couples the grid with kernel density estimation to reconstruct smooth radial distributions, validated on linear alkanes and the S22 dataset.

The multicenter grid is coupled with kernel density estimation to reconstruct smooth radial intracule distributions at large interelectronic distances without dense angular grids.

The partitioning enables decomposition of global two-electron properties into spatial contributions from short- and long-range electron-pair separations. AI.conclusion: These developments facilitate intracule analysis in polyatomic systems and the investigation of electron correlation and dispersion interactions.

title: Complex Magnetic Phases and Unconventional Skyrmion Thermodynamics in Magnetically Intercalated Cr$_{1+x}$Te$_2$Compounds
summary: Chemical intercalation provides a powerful route for tuning the electronic and magnetic properties of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), enabling the emergence of magnetic phases and phenomena that are otherwise inaccessible in their pristine forms. Here, we investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of magnetically intercalated Cr$_{1+x}$Te$_2$ through a combination of scanning tunneling microscopy, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, magnetization, electrical transport, and Lorentz transmission electron microscopy measurements. We uncover a rich magnetic phase diagram comprising paramagnetic, in-plane spin-fluctuation, out-of-plane ferromagnetic, and field-induced Néel-type skyrmion phases. In particular, Lorentz transmission electron microscopy directly reveals the formation of Néel-type skyrmion textures slightly below the Curie temperature, with their configurations evolving strongly with temperature and magnetic field. The skyrmions exhibit pronounced thermal hysteresis and coexist with stripe domains, indicative of a complex magnetic energy landscape arising from the competition among disorder-induced local Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, and dipolar interactions. Our results demonstrate that chemical intercalation can profoundly reshape the magnetic interactions and phase behavior of TMDs, establishing Cr$_{1+x}$Te$_2$ as a versatile platform for exploring tunable magnetism, skyrmion physics, and unconventional thermodynamic phenomena in low-dimensional quantum materials.

title: Local geometry of the Fermi surface and its effect on the electronic characteristics of normal metals
summary: Fine features in the Fermi surface geometry, such as nearly cylindrical or nearly paraboloidal strips or local flattenings, are examined as regards their effect on the electronic, mainly galvanomagnetic, properties of metals. It is shown that under certain conditions, these features may significantly change the way a conventional normal metal or a layered structure with metallic conductivity responds to high- frequency external disturbances. All of the effects considered appear to be very sensitive to the disturbance propagation direction and/or to that of the external magnetic field. Experimental possibilities of observing the described effects are discussed.

AI.tldr: Fine Fermi-surface geometry features (near-cylindrical/paraboloidal strips, local flattenings) can strongly and anisotropically alter the high-frequency galvanomagnetic response of metals and layered metallic conductors.
AI.motivation: Conventional treatments of electronic and galvanomagnetic properties often rely on idealized Fermi-surface shapes, neglecting finer geometrical details. The paper asks whether such fine features (near-cylindrical or near-paraboloidal strips, local flattenings) materially affect the response of normal metals and layered metallic structures.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of Fermi-surface geometry and its effect on electronic, mainly galvanomagnetic, properties; the fine features are treated as determinants of the response to high-frequency external disturbances, with explicit attention to the dependence on disturbance propagation direction and external magnetic field orientation. Experimental observation routes for the predicted effects are also examined.

The effects are found to be very sensitive to the propagation direction of the disturbance and/or the direction of the applied magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: Fine Fermi-surface geometry is a controlling factor for high-frequency galvanomagnetic behavior in metals and layered metallic conductors, producing strongly directional effects; the paper identifies these effects and discusses feasible experiments to observe them.

title: Inertial Dynamics of a Skymeron
summary: Topological spin textures in antiferromagnets inherit the compensated magnetic order of the host material, resulting for skyrmions in the suppression of the skyrmion Hall effect and enabling ultrafast dynamics that make them attractive for low-power spintronic devices. In intrinsic antiferromagnets, the two sublattices are identical, but synthetic antiferromagnets offer additional control mechanisms by enabling independent tuning of the properties of two ferromagnetic layers. Analogous to a ferrimagnet, the total magnetic moment can be adjusted by compensating the two-layer moments. Here, we demonstrate that tuning the effective magnetic anisotropy difference between the two layers drives a spin-flop transition where one layer reorients and thus stabilizes an orthogonal configuration with one layer oriented along the out-of-plane direction and the other in-plane. In this transition, an antiferromagnetic skyrmion undergoes a homotopic reconfiguration into a complex spin texture comprising a skyrmion coupled to an in-plane bimeron. Element-specific X-ray microscopy resolves this texture layer by layer: one hosts an out-of-plane skyrmion coupled to an in-plane bimeron in the other. We refer to this previously unexplored three-dimensional spin texture as a skymeron. By using time-resolved pump-probe X-ray microscopy, we discover unique polarity ,dependent dynamics during current pulses: a short post-pulse inertia-like continuation of the motion, and a slower return towards the pinned initial state. Micromagnetic simulations reveal that the inertia-like propagation originates from the finite-time relaxation of reorientation of the skymeron. Our results establish layer-selective anisotropy engineering as a route to uncharted composite spin textures with internal dynamical degrees of freedom, not possible in conventional antiferromagnets with identical sublattices.

AI.tldr: By tuning the effective anisotropy difference between the two layers of a synthetic antiferromagnet, an antiferromagnetic skyrmion homotopically reconfigures into a novel composite 3D spin texture—a "skymeron," comprising a skyrmion in one layer coupled to an in-plane bimeron in the other—which exhibits unique polarity-dependent current-driven dynamics with inertia-like post-pulse motion.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnetic skyrmions are attractive for low-power spintronics because compensated magnetic order suppresses the skyrmion Hall effect and enables ultrafast dynamics. However, intrinsic antiferromagnets have identical sublattices, limiting tunability. Synthetic antiferromagnets offer additional control by allowing independent tuning of two ferromagnetic layers, motivating the exploration of new composite spin textures and their dynamics.
