title: Tunable Electron Quantum Optics in Graphene Slit Junctions
summary: A graphene slit junction is investigated as a compact geometry for directional electron-beam formation, coherent interference, and symmetry-controlled spin filtering. Atomistic tight-binding calculations combined with the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism show that trigonal warping in monolayer graphene produces strongly directional electron beams near E~2.7eV. Boundary reflections redirect these beams toward a common drain, where the transmission exhibits magnetic flux-dependent oscillations consistent with an h/e Aharonov-Bohm period, whose modulation is characterized by Fourier analysis and harmonic fitting. A local electrostatic gate provides additional control of the interference phase. In separate self-consistent mean-field Hubbard calculations, the pristine antiferromagnetic ground state is shown to have spin-degenerate transmission, whereas structural or electrostatic breaking of the left-right symmetry enables spin filtering. Complementary valley-resolved calculations using a four-band continuum model demonstrate analogous beam formation in bilayer graphene at E = 50meV. The results identify the slit junction as a common geometry for electron-optical and spin-dependent transport and motivate further investigation of low-energy bilayer implementations.

AI.motivation: To explore a single compact geometry that can simultaneously achieve directional electron-beam formation, coherent interference control, and spin filtering, exploiting graphene's electronic and symmetry properties.
AI.method: Atomistic tight-binding calculations with the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism; Fourier analysis and harmonic fitting of flux-dependent transmission; self-consistent mean-field Hubbard calculations for spin transport; and valley-resolved four-band continuum-model calculations for bilayer graphene.
AI.result: Trigonal warping in monolayer graphene produces strongly directional electron beams near E ≈ 2.7 eV; boundary reflections redirect beams toward a common drain, giving transmission oscillations with an h/e Aharonov-Bohm period. A local electrostatic gate controls the interference phase. The pristine antiferromagnetic ground state shows spin-degenerate transmission, while structural or electrostatic breaking of left-right symmetry enables spin filtering. Bilayer graphene exhibits analogous beam formation at E = 50 meV.

title: Relativistic Hirshfeld atoms in a molecule: An information-theoretic view, with application to Drude oscillator dispersion models
summary: Several ad hoc dispersion models for density-functional theory are based on the use of Hirshfeld (or "stockholder") partition of a molecular charge density, which provides an in situ definition of atomic size. We show that a recently introduced "optimized" quantum Drude oscillator model for dispersion admits a closed-form solution in terms of the Lambert $W$ function, whose branches identify the compact and diffuse oscillator solutions. The compact solution determines the $C_8$ (dipole-quadrupole) dispersion coefficient analytically from the free-atom polarizability, $C_6$ coefficient, and van der Waals radius, without any reference $C_8$ data. Next, we provide a formal basis for a relativistic version of the atoms-in-molecule Hirshfeld partition. Using four-component Dirac-Hartree-Fock densities for isolated atoms defines a strictly positive deformation field that carries the relativistic changes in atomic density into the Hirshfeld partition. A uniqueness theorem for the non-relativistic case is extended to relativistic Hirshfeld atoms and admits an asymptotic expansion through quadratic order in the fine-structure constant. Normalization requires the relativistic density correction to reshape the reference atom while preserving its population. Finally, four-component polarizabilities and C6 coefficients are reported for closed-shell atoms and ions, which supply the reference data required to extend atoms-in-molecules dispersion models into the heavy-element regime. Periodic trends are observable in a scalar contraction factor that measures relativistic effects.

AI.tldr: A quantum Drude oscillator dispersion model yields an analytic C8 coefficient via the Lambert W function, and Hirshfeld atoms-in-molecule partitioning is extended to the relativistic regime using four-component Dirac-Hartree-Fock densities.
AI.motivation: Ad hoc DFT dispersion models rely on Hirshfeld (stockholder) partitioning of molecular charge density to define atomic size in situ, but they lack a closed-form dispersion treatment and a relativistic foundation needed for heavy elements.
AI.method: A recent "optimized" quantum Drude oscillator model is solved in closed form using the Lambert W function, whose branches distinguish compact and diffuse solutions. A relativistic Hirshfeld partition is constructed using four-component Dirac-Hartree-Fock densities of isolated atoms, defining a strictly positive deformation field; a non-relativistic uniqueness theorem is extended to the relativistic case with an asymptotic expansion through quadratic order in the fine-structure constant, with normalization reshaping the reference atom while preserving population.

Four-component polarizabilities and C6 coefficients are reported for closed-shell atoms and ions, with periodic trends visible in a scalar contraction factor quantifying relativistic effects.
AI.conclusion: The Lambert W formulation provides reference-free C8 coefficients, and the relativistic Hirshfeld atoms-in-molecule framework supplies the reference data needed to extend dispersion models into the heavy-element regime.

title: Topological robustness of thermally disordered lattices: From average structures to ensemble electronic properties
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures. Data available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23067045
summary: Band topology is usually assigned to a single crystal structure, yet at finite temperature a crystal is an ensemble of thermally disordered configurations with a fluctuating band gap. We ask whether the thermally averaged structure is a faithful proxy for this ensemble, taking Bi$_2$Se$_3$ as a representative topological insulator and classifying band ordering in each ab initio molecular dynamics snapshot by scaling the spin-orbit coupling. The averaged structure fails in two ways: it misses the Rashba-like spin splitting that instantaneous symmetry breaking produces in individual configurations, and it substantially underestimates the band-gap renormalization, whereas a small ensemble of harmonic Monte Carlo configurations reproduces both the mean and the spread of the gap. Using a band-inversion survival probability, we find that the band inversion of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ holds in every sampled configuration up to 600 K, above which individual configurations cross into normal band ordering well before the average gap closes. Topological robustness at finite temperature is thus a property of the distribution over configurations rather than of any single structure.

AI.tldr: Thermal disorder in Bi2Se3 is captured by an ensemble of ab initio MD snapshots; the averaged structure is an unfaithful proxy, missing Rashba splitting and underestimating gap renormalization, while band inversion survives in every configuration up to 600 K.
AI.motivation: Band topology is conventionally assigned to a single crystal structure, but at finite temperature a crystal is an ensemble of thermally disordered configurations with a fluctuating band gap. The paper asks whether the thermally averaged structure is a faithful proxy for this ensemble.
AI.method: Using Bi2Se3 as a representative topological insulator, the authors classify band ordering in each ab initio molecular dynamics snapshot by scaling the spin-orbit coupling. They compare the averaged structure against instantaneous configurations and against a small ensemble of harmonic Monte Carlo configurations, and introduce a band-inversion survival probability.
AI.result: The averaged structure fails in two ways: it misses the Rashba-like spin splitting produced by instantaneous symmetry breaking in individual configurations, and it substantially underestimates band-gap renormalization. A small ensemble of harmonic Monte Carlo configurations reproduces both the mean and the spread of the gap. Using the band-inversion survival probability, the band inversion of Bi2Se3 holds in every sampled configuration up to 600 K, above which individual configurations cross into normal band ordering well before the average gap closes.

title: Robustness of the Verwey transition against remanent strain-induced defects in magnetite
summary: The Verwey transition in magnetite is a benchmark electronically driven phase transition that is highly sensitive to lattice imperfections and external perturbations. Doping, deviations from oxygen stoichiometry, and irradiation-induced point defects are known to lower the Verwey transition temperature, $T_{\rm V}$. By contrast, the role of remanent strain fields and extended defect structures generated by uniaxial stress has remained largely unexplored. Here we combine dark-field x-ray microscopy (DFXM) and ac magnetic susceptibility to determine how strain-induced defects affect the Verwey transition in stoichiometric single-crystalline magnetite after uniaxial compression and unloading. The DFXM measurements were performed on two samples compressed along the same $[011]$ direction: loading to $200~\mathrm{MPa}$ generated stable line-like defects and remanent strain fields, whereas loading beyond the fracture threshold produced denser defect networks and mechanical fracture. To test the effect of a different loading geometry, we also measured the ac susceptibility of a sample fractured by compression along $[001]$. Real-space DFXM imaging, lattice-orientation mapping, and residual strain mapping show substantial remanent structural disorder after compression. Nevertheless, neither the transition temperature $T_{\rm V}$ nor the sharpness of the transition changes measurably in any of the compressed or fractured samples. This behavior contrasts with the strong suppression of $T_{\rm V}$ by point-like disorder. Our results show that extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields produced by plastic deformation do not measurably perturb the macroscopic electronic ordering responsible for the Verwey transition, thereby distinguishing the effects of point defects from those of extended slip-related defects in magnetite.

AI.tldr: Uniaxial compression and fracture of stoichiometric magnetite create extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields (revealed by dark-field x-ray microscopy) but leave the Verwey transition temperature and its sharpness unchanged, unlike point-like disorder which strongly suppresses T_V.
AI.motivation: The Verwey transition in magnetite is an electronically driven phase transition sensitive to lattice imperfections and external perturbations. While doping, oxygen non-stoichiometry, and irradiation-induced point defects are known to lower T_V, the role of remanent strain fields and extended defect structures generated by uniaxial stress has remained largely unexplored.
AI.method: Combined dark-field x-ray microscopy (DFXM) and ac magnetic susceptibility measurements on stoichiometric single-crystalline magnetite after uniaxial compression and unloading. Two samples were compressed along [011]: loading to 200 MPa (generating stable line-like defects and remanent strain fields) and loading beyond the fracture threshold (producing denser defect networks and mechanical fracture). A sample fractured by compression along [001] was also measured to test a different loading geometry. DFXM provided real-space imaging, lattice-orientation mapping, and residual strain mapping.

However, neither the transition temperature T_V nor the sharpness of the transition changed measurably in any of the compressed or fractured samples, in strong contrast to the suppression of T_V by point-like disorder.
AI.conclusion: Extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields produced by plastic deformation do not measurably perturb the macroscopic electronic ordering responsible for the Verwey transition, distinguishing the effects of point defects from those of extended slip-related defects in magnetite.

title: Dynamical Critical Properties of the Random-Bond three-state Potts Model
summary: We study the dynamic critical behavior of the two-dimensional random-bond three-state Potts model using large-scale Monte Carlo simulations with the Wolff and Swendsen--Wang cluster algorithms. At the disorder-dependent critical temperature, we compute integrated and exponential autocorrelation times and extract the dynamic critical exponent $z$ via finite-size scaling. Critical slowing down is significantly weakened by bond randomness, with the dynamic exponent decreasing from $z \approx 0.54$ in the pure system to $z \approx 0.24$ at strong disorder. From the finite-size scaling of the Wolff cluster size, we obtain $γ/ν\approx 1.73$, where $γ$ and $ν$ are the susceptibility and correlation-length exponents, respectively, consistent with the universality class of the two-dimensional three-state Potts model. These results indicate that bond randomness strongly affects the critical dynamics but leaves the underlying static universality class unchanged. Furthermore, both static and dynamic observables, including the specific heat and the autocorrelation times, show a lack of self-averaging.

AI.tldr: Bond randomness in the 2D three-state Potts model strongly weakens critical slowing down (z drops from ~0.54 to ~0.24) while leaving the static universality class unchanged; self-averaging is absent.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how quenched bond disorder influences the dynamic critical behavior of the two-dimensional three-state Potts model, a question of interest for distinguishing universal dynamic properties from disorder-specific effects.
AI.method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations using Wolff and Swendsen-Wang cluster algorithms at the disorder-dependent critical temperature; integrated and exponential autocorrelation times and the dynamic critical exponent z are extracted via finite-size scaling, with γ/ν obtained from the Wolff cluster-size scaling.
AI.result: Critical slowing down is significantly weakened by bond randomness, with z decreasing from z ≈ 0.54 in the pure system to z ≈ 0.24 at strong disorder. The ratio γ/ν ≈ 1.73 agrees with the 2D three-state Potts universality class. Both static and dynamic observables (specific heat, autocorrelation times) show a lack of self-averaging.
AI.conclusion: Bond randomness strongly affects critical dynamics but leaves the underlying static universality class unchanged, and the model exhibits non-self-averaging behavior in both static and dynamic quantities.

title: Benchmarking average atom potentials derived from atomic cluster expansions
summary: Average atom (A-atom) potentials provide a mean-field description of a chemically disordered alloy and are used to predict the properties of solid solutions without short-range order. Such potentials are usually averaged from an existing interatomic potential and are therefore only as accurate as the parent model. Accurate interatomic potentials are themselves difficult to parameterize and can require large training datasets. Here we benchmark a recently developed formalism that computes an exact A-atom potential directly from a linear atomic cluster expansion (ACE). We first fit a linear ACE to Fe-W data generated with an embedded atom method (EAM) potential. The resulting A-atom potential reproduces the properties of the disordered phase computed from an explicit random supercell and from a conventional A-atom potential averaged from the same EAM potential. We then fit a linear ACE to energies and forces computed from electronic structure calculations for about 1500 small Mo-Nb structures with an average of 7 atoms per structure. The A-atom potential derived from this ACE reproduces the DFT elastic constants, lattice parameter, mixing enthalpy, and Bain path of special quasirandom structures. Of the three chemical site bases, only the occupation basis also reproduces the DFT surface energies of the alloy. For Mo-Nb, the A-atom potential also predicts that the ideal solution entropy outweighs the destabilizing vibrational contribution to the finite-temperature free energy of the disordered phase. These benchmarks show that the properties of disordered alloys can be recovered from small training datasets when the chemical site basis is chosen carefully.

AI.tldr: A linear atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is used to compute exact average-atom potentials for chemically disordered alloys, recovering DFT and EAM benchmark properties from small training datasets.
AI.motivation: Average atom potentials offer a mean-field description of chemically disordered alloys but are conventionally averaged from existing interatomic potentials, inheriting their accuracy limits. Accurate interatomic potentials are hard to parameterize and demand large training datasets, motivating a direct, exact route from a linear ACE.
AI.method: The authors benchmark a recently developed formalism that computes an exact A-atom potential directly from a linear ACE. First, a linear ACE is fitted to Fe-W data from an EAM potential. Then, a linear ACE is fitted to energies and forces from electronic structure calculations for ~1500 small Mo-Nb structures (avg. 7 atoms). The derived A-atom potentials are compared against explicit random supercells, conventional averaged EAM-based A-atom potentials, and DFT reference quantities (elastic constants, lattice parameter, mixing enthalpy, Bain path, surface energies, finite-temperature free energy). Three chemical site bases are tested.
AI.result: For Fe-W, the ACE-derived A-atom potential reproduces disordered-phase properties from an explicit random supercell and from a conventional averaged EAM A-atom potential. For Mo-Nb, the ACE-derived A-atom potential reproduces DFT elastic constants, lattice parameter, mixing enthalpy, and the Bain path of special quasirandom structures. Only the occupation basis among the three chemical site bases also reproduces DFT surface energies. The Mo-Nb A-atom potential predicts that ideal solution entropy outweighs the destabilizing vibrational contribution to the finite-temperature free energy of the disordered phase.
AI.conclusion: Properties of disordered alloys can be recovered from small training datasets when the chemical site basis is chosen carefully, enabling accurate A-atom potentials without large training data or parent-potential inheritance.

title: Hydrogen plasma-assisted atomic layer epitaxy of superconducting titanium nitride
summary: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) offers precise, conformal control of thin-film growth and is a workhorse for semiconductor manufacturing, but its use in superconducting quantum circuits is constrained by the need to simultaneously control crystallinity, stoichiometry and interfacial disorder at cryogenic temperatures. Here we develop hydrogen plasma assisted ALD to epitaxially grow superconducting titanium nitride (TiN) thin films, using a hydrogen plasma step to modify the surface chemistry to suppress precursor-derived impurities during each deposition cycle. Synchrotron X-ray scattering reveals semi-coherent epitaxy of TiN on c-plane sapphire, with discrete crystallographic domains and minimal long-range structural disorder. Complementary X-ray spectroscopy and neutron reflectometry show negligible oxygen-related disorder throughout the film and no substantial hydrogen incorporation. The resulting TiN films exhibit a superconducting transition at 2.2 K, a kinetic inductance of 15 pH/sq and a superconducting coherence length of 14.6 nm, comparable to the measured crystal coherence length. These results establish hydrogen plasma assisted ALD as a route to structurally ordered superconducting TiN thin film epitaxy and demonstrate that the nanoscale control of ALD can be extended to materials suitable for cryogenic quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: Hydrogen plasma assisted ALD enables epitaxial superconducting TiN films on sapphire with low disorder and competitive superconducting properties.
AI.motivation: ALD is valuable for precise, conformal thin-film growth in semiconductor manufacturing, but its application to superconducting quantum circuits is limited by the difficulty of simultaneously controlling crystallinity, stoichiometry, and interfacial disorder at cryogenic temperatures.
AI.method: The authors develop hydrogen plasma assisted ALD to epitaxially grow superconducting TiN thin films, introducing a hydrogen plasma step each deposition cycle to modify surface chemistry and suppress precursor-derived impurities. Films were characterized by synchrotron X-ray scattering, X-ray spectroscopy, and neutron reflectometry.
AI.result: Synchrotron X-ray scattering shows semi-coherent TiN epitaxy on c-plane sapphire with discrete crystallographic domains and minimal long-range structural disorder. Spectroscopy and neutron reflectometry reveal negligible oxygen-related disorder and no substantial hydrogen incorporation. The films exhibit a superconducting transition at 2.2 K, kinetic inductance of 15 pH/sq, and superconducting coherence length of 14.6 nm, comparable to the crystal coherence length.

title: Layer-by-layer growth of highly aligned MoS$_2$ nanoribbon arrays
summary: One-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD) nanoribbons (NRs) offer a promising route to aggressive channel-width scaling in nanoscale transistors. However, controlling their layer number, a key determinant of device performance, has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate a chemical vapor deposition (CVD) approach for layer-by-layer growth of MoS$_2$ NRs on a low-symmetry sapphire surface. This approach enables the oriented growth of single-crystalline bilayer NRs with a 2H stacking configuration, while maintaining widths below 20 nm. Increasing the MoO$_3$ precursor supply was found to be crucial for promoting the growth of the second and subsequent layers. By controlling the growth time and precursor supply, the layer number of MoS$_2$ NRs can be increased up to four layers. This method can also be extended to the growth of vertical MoS$_2$/WS$_2$ hetero-NRs. The average carrier mobility and current density of bilayer NR field-effect transistors (FETs) are two- and three-times higher than those of monolayer counterparts, respectively, and a maximum mobility of 86.7 cm$^2$V$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$ was attained with a bilayer NR-FET. These results highlight layer number as a key parameter for optimizing NR device performance. Our thickness-controlled growth strategy provides a general route towards TMD NR-based transistors with enhanced scalability and performance.

AI.tldr: A CVD method enables layer-by-layer growth of MoS2 nanoribbons (up to 4 layers) on low-symmetry sapphire, with bilayer nanoribbon FETs showing 2-3x higher mobility and current density than monolayers (max mobility 86.7 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹).
AI.motivation: 1D TMD nanoribbons are promising for channel-width scaling in nanoscale transistors, but controlling their layer number—a key determinant of device performance—has remained elusive.
AI.method: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) for layer-by-layer growth of MoS2 nanoribbons on a low-symmetry sapphire surface; increasing MoO3 precursor supply promotes growth of the second and subsequent layers, and controlling growth time and precursor supply tunes layer number up to four. The method is also extended to vertical MoS2/WS2 hetero-nanoribbons.
AI.result: Oriented, single-crystalline bilayer nanoribbons with 2H stacking and widths below 20 nm were obtained. Bilayer NR-FETs exhibited average carrier mobility and current density 2- and 3-times higher than monolayer counterparts, respectively, with a maximum mobility of 86.7 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: Layer number is a key parameter for optimizing nanoribbon device performance, and this thickness-controlled growth strategy offers a general route toward TMD NR-based transistors with enhanced scalability and performance.

title: Na$_2$Ir$^\text{IV}$Cl$_6$: The Missing Member of the Perfectly Cubic Vacancy Ordered $A_2$IrCl$_6$ Family, Another Potential $J_{eff}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ Ground State Candidate
summary: Vacancy ordered double perovskites (VODPs) have been known for more than 100 years, but their exact crystal structures and magnetic ground state remained controversial till date. Anhydrous VODP iridates ($A_2$Ir$X_6$; $A$ = K$^+$, (NH$_4$)$^+$, Cs$^+$, Rb$^+$, and $X$ = F$^-$, Cl$^-$, Br$^-$), having $face-centered~cubic$ (fcc) antiferromagnetic ground state, offer a chemically well-defined platform to investigate the influence of on-site Coulomb repulsion, crystal field, spin-orbit coupling, and competing Heisenberg and Kitaev interactions. Interestingly, among these, the Na-based VODP iridates seem to possess an unusual hydration dependent structural and magnetic uncertainty. As a result, a cubic Na$_2$IrCl$_6$ system having fcc antiferromagnetism could not be stabilized ever. Here, for the first time, we report the synthesis and comprehensive characterization of anhydrous Na$_2$IrCl$_6$ single crystals having fcc structure with antiferromagnetic transition temperature of 1.91 K. Thermogravimetric analysis establishes the absence of lattice water and also demonstrates thermal stability of the crystals up to 453 K. The cubic phase reported here contrasts with previously described 'anhydrous' monoclinic Na$_2$IrCl$_6$ and highlights the strong structural and physical property relationship in Na-based VODP iridates. This new material offers an exciting playing ground for exploring another potential perfect $J_{eff}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ octahedra and the consequent strong Kitaev interaction within the nearest-neighbor (nn) pairs of Ir ions.

AI.tldr: First synthesis of anhydrous cubic Na2IrCl6 single crystals with fcc structure and antiferromagnetic ordering at 1.91 K, resolving long-standing hydration-dependent structural ambiguity in Na-based vacancy ordered double perovskite iridates.
AI.motivation: Vacancy ordered double perovskites (VODPs) have been known for over a century, yet their exact crystal structures and magnetic ground states remain controversial. Anhydrous VODP iridates with fcc antiferromagnetic ground states serve as chemically well-defined platforms to study on-site Coulomb repulsion, crystal field, spin-orbit coupling, and competing Heisenberg and Kitaev interactions. However, Na-based VODP iridates exhibit unusual hydration-dependent structural and magnetic uncertainty, and a cubic Na2IrCl6 system with fcc antiferromagnetism had never been stabilized.
AI.method: Synthesis and comprehensive characterization of anhydrous Na2IrCl6 single crystals. Structural determination was performed to establish the fcc cubic phase, and magnetic measurements identified the antiferromagnetic transition. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was used to confirm the absence of lattice water and to assess thermal stability.
AI.result: Anhydrous Na2IrCl6 single crystals were synthesized with an fcc structure and an antiferromagnetic transition temperature of 1.91 K. title: Work fluctuation speed limit in boundary conformal field theories
summary: We explore the fundamental limits on finite-time driving in quantum critical systems described by boundary conformal field theory. We show that stochastic work fluctuations arising from external driving are a resource for speedy control, and derive an exact, saturable fluctuation-based speed limit in weakly driven boundary conformal field theories at finite temperature. The bound and saturating protocol can be expressed entirely in terms of the universal scaling dimension, and the result interpolates between the Kibble--Zurek regime,where temporal correlations are strongly nonlocal, and an adiabatic regime where linear driving becomes optimal. For small scaling dimension, the enhanced temporal correlations produce pronounced departures from linear protocols and a larger optimization advantage. These results establish a universal work precision--time tradeoff for boundary-critical control, applicable to quantum impurity, fractional quantum Hall, and superconducting-circuit platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact, saturable fluctuation-based speed limit for weakly driven boundary conformal field theories at finite temperature, showing stochastic work fluctuations act as a resource for fast control, with results governed solely by the universal scaling dimension.
AI.motivation: Finite-time driving in quantum critical systems faces fundamental speed limits, yet how work fluctuations and nonlocal temporal correlations constrain and enable speedy control in boundary-critical settings remains unclear. The authors aim to establish universal limits and optimal protocols for such control.
AI.method: They analyze weakly driven boundary conformal field theory at finite temperature, deriving an exact fluctuation-based speed limit from stochastic work fluctuations and constructing a saturating driving protocol expressed in terms of the universal scaling dimension.
AI.result: An exact, saturable speed limit is obtained, with the bound and saturating protocol entirely given by the universal scaling dimension. The result interpolates between the Kibble-Zurek regime with strongly nonlocal temporal correlations and an adiabatic regime where linear driving is optimal; small scaling dimensions yield pronounced departures from linear protocols and larger optimization advantage.
AI.conclusion: A universal work precision-time tradeoff for boundary-critical control is established, applicable to quantum impurity, fractional quantum Hall, and superconducting-circuit platforms.

title: Charge and spin dynamics in spintronic THz emitters from Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
summary: Spintronic terahertz (THz) emitters based on ferromagnet/heavy-metal heterostructures provide efficient broadband sources of THz radiation, yet the microscopic relation between ultrafast spin transport and charge redistribution remains incompletely understood. Here, we employ time-dependent density functional theory to resolve the coupled charge, spin, and magnetization dynamics of Co/Pt and Co/W bilayers in real time and space. Despite qualitatively similar interlayer spin-current dynamics, the two heterostructures exhibit markedly different interlayer charge transfer: Co/Pt shows a relatively small and partially reversed transfer from Pt to Co, whereas Co/W exhibits a larger and persistent transfer from Co to W. We trace these differences to the material-dependent ground-state electronic structure and the spin- and orbital-resolved phase space accessible to photoexcited carriers. Spin-resolved dynamics further reveal coexisting spin-orbit-mediated redistribution and optically induced intersite spin transfer, including a delayed minority-spin transfer from the heavy metal to Co common to both systems. While net electronic spin angular momentum is transferred between the layers, we find no corresponding net transfer of electronic orbital angular momentum. In Co/W, the persistent redistribution of electronic density from interstitial to atom-centered states additionally provides strong evidence for light-induced electronic localization. These results demonstrate that ultrafast spin transport does not uniquely determine charge or angular-momentum redistribution in spintronic THz emitters, which instead depends critically on the material-specific electronic phase space.

AI.motivation: Spintronic THz emitters based on ferromagnet/heavy-metal bilayers are efficient broadband sources, but the microscopic link between ultrafast spin transport and charge redistribution is poorly understood, limiting rational design.
AI.method: Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) is used to resolve coupled charge, spin, and magnetization dynamics of Co/Pt and Co/W bilayers in real time and real space, with spin- and orbital-resolved analysis of photoexcited carrier phase space and ground-state electronic structure.
AI.result: Interlayer spin-current dynamics are qualitatively similar, but interlayer charge transfer differs strongly: Co/Pt shows small, partially reversed Pt-to-Co transfer, while Co/W shows larger, persistent Co-to-W transfer. Both systems exhibit coexisting spin-orbit-mediated redistribution and optically induced intersite spin transfer, including a delayed minority-spin transfer from heavy metal to Co. Net electronic spin angular momentum transfers between layers, but no net orbital angular momentum transfer occurs. Co/W shows strong evidence of light-induced electronic localization via persistent redistribution from interstitial to atom-centered states.
AI.conclusion: Ultrafast spin transport does not uniquely determine charge or angular-momentum redistribution in spintronic THz emitters; instead, these depend critically on material-specific electronic phase space and ground-state electronic structure.

title: PyCDFT: A Python-scriptable library for analytical evaluation of orbital conceptual density (matrix) functional theory
summary: Conceptual density functional theory (CDFT) defines chemical reactivity descriptors as derivatives of the electronic energy with respect to the number of electrons and the external potential, or combinations thereof; in practice, however, researchers almost always replace these derivatives with finite-difference and frontier-orbital approximations, and no common software exists for their analytical evaluation. We present PyCDFT, to our knowledge, the first standardized, open-source, and scriptable code that analytically computes the descriptors of conceptual density (matrix) functional theory for ground and excited states up to second order, including the orbital hardness, the Fukui function and Fukui matrix, and the linear response function, from a single converged mean-field wavefunction imported from virtually any electronic-structure package. The descriptors are obtained from matrix-free, preconditioned Krylov-subspace solutions of the coupled-perturbed self-consistent-field equations for both spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized references, with the work distributed over MPI ranks and all data flowing through a single HDF5 checkpoint file that supports restart, post-processing, and the export of real-space descriptors as cube files for visualization. The design delegates integrals, grids, and exchange-correlation kernels to PySCF and Libxc, keeping the library compact, user-friendly, and interoperable. Worked examples on the ground state of H$_2$O and a broken-symmetry $Δ$SCF excited state of NH$_3$ show that a complete second-order CDFT analysis requires only a few lines of user code.

AI.motivation: Conceptual density functional theory (CDFT) defines chemical reactivity descriptors as derivatives of electronic energy with respect to electron number and external potential. In practice, these derivatives are almost always replaced by finite-difference and frontier-orbital approximations, and no common software exists for their analytical evaluation. This work addresses that gap by providing an analytical, standardized computational tool.
AI.method: PyCDFT analytically computes conceptual density (matrix) functional theory descriptors for ground and excited states up to second order, including orbital hardness, the Fukui function and Fukui matrix, and the linear response function, starting from a single converged mean-field wavefunction imported from virtually any electronic-structure package. AI.result: Worked examples on the ground state of H2O and a broken-symmetry ΔSCF excited state of NH3 demonstrate that a complete second-order CDFT analysis requires only a few lines of user code, confirming the code's compactness, user-friendliness, and interoperability.

title: Room-temperature Magnetoelastic Coupling in UIr$_4$Al$_{15}$
summary: The interplay between electronic and structural degrees of freedom underpins many emergent phenomena in quantum materials, yet magnetoelastic coupling in metallic systems is typically weak and confined to low temperatures or microscopic length scales. Here, we report giant magnetoelastic coupling slightly above room temperature in the uranium-based intermetallic compound UIr$_4$Al$_{15}$. Using temperature-dependent single-crystal X-ray diffraction together with anisotropic magnetic susceptibility measurements, we directly resolve subtle but reproducible structural distortions coupled to magnetic alignment. Despite the absence of crystallographic symmetry breaking, pronounced anomalies emerge in lattice parameters and selected chemical bond distances near the magnetic transition region, revealing an unusual sensitivity of the crystal structure to magnetic orientation. The coupling enables direct probing of how atomic distances and local chemical bonding govern the electronic and magnetic states in a bulk intermetallic material. Our results establish UIr$_4$Al$_{15}$ as a rare platform in which magnetism and lattice distortions are strongly intertwined near room temperature, opening new opportunities for magnetically responsive quantum materials and functional magnetic sensing applications.

AI.tldr: The paper reports giant magnetoelastic coupling slightly above room temperature in the uranium-based intermetallic UIr4Al15, where subtle but reproducible lattice distortions couple to magnetic alignment without crystallographic symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: Magnetoelastic coupling in metallic systems is typically weak and confined to low temperatures or microscopic length scales. The authors aim to identify a bulk metallic platform where magnetism and lattice distortions are strongly intertwined near room temperature.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent single-crystal X-ray diffraction combined with anisotropic magnetic susceptibility measurements on UIr4Al15 single crystals.
AI.result: Pronounced anomalies in lattice parameters and selected chemical bond distances appear near the magnetic transition region, despite no crystallographic symmetry breaking, revealing unusual sensitivity of the crystal structure to magnetic orientation and establishing giant magnetoelastic coupling slightly above room temperature.
AI.conclusion: UIr4Al15 is a rare bulk intermetallic platform with strongly intertwined magnetism and lattice distortions near room temperature, enabling direct probing of how atomic distances and local bonding govern electronic and magnetic states, with opportunities for magnetically responsive quantum materials and functional magnetic sensing.

title: On thermalization in random free fermions: Statistical origins and energy-dependent ETH structure
summary: We study the thermalization in the random free fermion model by a detailed random-matrix analysis. By computing the ensemble average and fluctuations of $\operatorname{Tr}(Aρ(t))$ for a single-particle observable $A$, we derive the thermalization function $g^2(t/τ_λ)$ with $τ_λ= \hbar/(2η\sqrt{N})$, prove its $|t|^{-3}$ asymptotic decay, and show that the variance of the fluctuations vanishes as $O(1/N)$ in the thermodynamic limit.Particle number conservation is also incorporated into the model, by which we further study the energy-shell eigenstate statistics and prove a factorization theorem of the eigenstate statistics. We further show that under a controlled eigenvector-eigenvalue correlation deformation, the diagonal energy-resolved slope and the off-diagonal eigenstate thermalization hypothesis spectral function acquire an energy dependence.Finally, we compute the fluctuations of correlation functions and compare the fluctuation scales with those of a fully chaotic system, revealing quantitative differences rooted in the Gaussian nature of the eigenstates.Our work establishes the random free fermion model as an analytically solvable realization of weak eigenstate thermalization hypothesis type self-averaging, and as a controllable setting in which eigenbasis chaos can be separated from spectral chaos.

AI.motivation: The random free fermion model offers a tractable setting to probe thermalization and eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) physics, yet a detailed random-matrix characterization of its thermalization dynamics and eigenstate statistics—especially separating eigenbasis chaos from spectral chaos—had been lacking.
AI.method: The authors perform a detailed random-matrix analysis, computing the ensemble average and fluctuations of Tr(Aρ(t)) for a single-particle observable A. They derive the thermalization function g²(t/τ_λ) with τ_λ = ℏ/(2η√N), establish its |t|⁻³ asymptotic decay, and show the fluctuation variance vanishes as O(1/N). Particle number conservation is incorporated to study energy-shell eigenstate statistics and prove a factorization theorem. A controlled eigenvector-eigenvalue correlation deformation is introduced to examine energy dependence of the diagonal energy-resolved slope and the off-diagonal ETH spectral function. Correlation-function fluctuations are computed and compared with a fully chaotic system.
AI.result: The thermalization function g²(t/τ_λ) is obtained with τ_λ = ℏ/(2η√N) and proven to decay as |t|⁻³, with fluctuation variance vanishing as O(1/N) in the thermodynamic limit. Particle number conservation yields a factorization theorem for eigenstate statistics. title: Gate Dispersive Charge Detection in Ge/SiGe Quantum Dots
summary: Spin qubits are an attractive platform for scalable quantum information processing, and recently, laterally gated quantum dots (QDs) in Ge heterostructures have emerged as a leading implementation of spin qubits. To date, RF single-hole transistors (SHT) and integrated superconducting resonators have been used for spin and charge readout, but their size can pose challenges. Here we demonstrate compact RF gate-dispersive charge readout of a Ge double QD (DQD), and a single hole box (SHB)-DQD system. We resolve QD loading and interdot transitions with both techniques. We find that the SHB enhances the interdot signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of our 540 MHz circuit by a factor of 20 for a DQD coupling $t_c \approx 5$ GHz, providing a unity-SNR at 135 microseconds, c.f. for 2.7 miliseconds for the direct detection. Power- and temperature-dependent measurements verify that SNR is limited by dielectric loss which compromises impedance matching. These results establish a compact readout approach based on gate-dispersive detection for Ge/SiGe heterostructure QDs.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of compact RF gate-dispersive charge readout for a Ge double quantum dot and a single-hole-box (SHB)-DQD system, where the SHB boosts interdot SNR by 20x at 540 MHz.
AI.motivation: Spin qubits in Ge heterostructures are promising for scalable quantum information processing, but existing readout via RF single-hole transistors and integrated superconducting resonators is bulky; a more compact readout approach is needed.
AI.method: RF gate-dispersive charge readout applied to a Ge double quantum dot (DQD) and a single-hole-box (SHB)-DQD system, resolving QD loading and interdot transitions with both techniques, with power- and temperature-dependent measurements to identify SNR-limiting mechanisms.
AI.result: The SHB enhances the interdot SNR of the 540 MHz circuit by a factor of 20 for DQD coupling t_c ≈ 5 GHz, achieving unity SNR at 135 microseconds versus 2.7 milliseconds for direct detection. SNR is limited by dielectric loss compromising impedance matching.
AI.conclusion: A compact gate-dispersive readout approach is established for Ge/SiGe heterostructure quantum dots.

title: Nonadiabatic Quantum Dynamics of Hexatriene via the Extended Hubbard-Peierls Model and Time-Dependent DMRG
summary: Propagating the electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom of a molecule simultaneously is a challenging task, because the number of vibronic states grows exponentially with system size. We use the adaptive time-dependent density matrix renormalization group to perform simulations of the extended Hubbard-Peierls Hamiltonian, in which both the electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom are quantized. We describe our approach, and demonstrate it through converged calculations of the nonadiabatic dynamics of hexatriene. This simulation predicts a lifetime of the `bright' $\mathrm{1B_u}$ electronic state of approximately 40 fs. Our predictions for the population of the $\mathrm{1B_u}$ electronic state are in qualitative agreement with those obtained using the linear vibronic coupling model derived from the extended Hubbard-Peierls Hamiltonian in previous work.

AI.tldr: The authors apply adaptive time-dependent DMRG to simulate nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with both electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom quantized, using the extended Hubbard-Peierls Hamiltonian, demonstrated on hexatriene.
AI.motivation: Simultaneously propagating electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom is challenging because the number of vibronic states grows exponentially with system size, making exact treatment infeasible for larger molecules.
AI.method: Adaptive time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) simulations of the extended Hubbard-Peierls Hamiltonian with quantized electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom, applied to hexatriene and compared with prior linear vibronic coupling model results.
AI.result: Converged nonadiabatic dynamics of hexatriene were obtained, predicting a lifetime of the bright 1B_u electronic state of approximately 40 fs. The predicted 1B_u populations agree qualitatively with those from the linear vibronic coupling model derived previously from the extended Hubbard-Peierls Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive tDMRG provides a viable route to converged simulation of coupled electron-nuclear (vibronic) dynamics in molecules, and its results are consistent with linear vibronic coupling treatments for hexatriene.

title: Train for Accuracy, Execute at Scale: Architecture-Preserving Inference for Equivariant Atomistic Foundation Models
summary: Equivariant atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable interatomic potentials trained against quantum-mechanical reference data, but their repeated execution at simulation scale remains computationally and memory intensive. We present Symmetrix-XL, an inference engine that scales pretrained MACE checkpoints without retraining, distillation, or modification of their learned weights. It combines streamed-edge execution to avoid graph-wide materialization of expanded edge intermediates, model-specialized code generation to compile checkpoint-specific operators, and tiled execution to reuse a bounded device-memory workspace. On complete LAMMPS-step benchmarks, Symmetrix-XL reduces inference time by 3.1-5.0 times relative to ML-IAP + cuEquivariance across tested A100 and RTX 5090 workloads. On a single A100 80 GB GPU, the tested MACE-OMAT-0 capacity boundary increases from 24,565 atoms to 11.24 million atoms. This substantially lowers the hardware threshold for simulations that would otherwise require spatial decomposition across many GPUs and compute nodes. The same backend weak-scales to 703 million atoms on 64 A800 GPUs at 93.8 percent efficiency. Energy, force, stress, molecular-dynamics stability, and Matbench Discovery evaluations reproduce reference MACE behavior within measured tolerances. Case studies spanning solid-state, interfacial, and reactive systems demonstrate the increased capacity in realistic workflows. These results establish post-training execution as a scaling axis complementary to model redesign, compression, and distributed scale-out, and show that the practical accuracy-cost frontier depends on both model architecture and inference execution.

AI.tldr: Symmetrix-XL is an inference engine that accelerates pretrained MACE atomistic foundation models without retraining or weight modification, via streamed-edge execution, model-specialized code generation, and tiled execution, achieving 3.1-5.0x speedups and scaling single-GPU capacity from 24,565 to 11.24 million atoms.
AI.motivation: Equivariant atomistic foundation models such as MACE offer broadly transferable interatomic potentials, but their repeated execution at simulation scale is computationally and memory intensive, limiting practical accessibility.
AI.method: The paper introduces Symmetrix-XL, an inference engine that scales pretrained MACE checkpoints without retraining, distillation, or modification of learned weights. It combines three techniques: streamed-edge execution to avoid graph-wide materialization of expanded edge intermediates, model-specialized code generation to compile checkpoint-specific operators, and tiled execution to reuse a bounded device-memory workspace.

On a single A100 80 GB GPU, the MACE-OMAT-0 capacity boundary rises from 24,565 to 11.24 million atoms. The backend weak-scales to 703 million atoms on 64 A800 GPUs at 93.8% efficiency. Energy, force, stress, MD stability, and Matbench Discovery evaluations reproduce reference MACE behavior within tolerance, and case studies span solid-state, interfacial, and reactive systems.
AI.conclusion: Post-training execution is established as a scaling axis complementary to model redesign, compression, and distributed scale-out, and the practical accuracy-cost frontier depends on both model architecture and inference execution. This substantially lowers the hardware threshold for simulations otherwise requiring spatial decomposition across many GPUs and compute nodes.

title: Mass-asymmetry-controlled exciton dressing and dissociation in a quantum lattice model
summary: In a polar material, a neutral exciton couples to phonons through the sum of the electron and hole deformation potentials. Because the total source vanishes by charge neutrality, the elastic exciton-phonon vertex is regularized by electron-hole interference. Here we determine the non-perturbative fate of this interference by exact diagonalization of a Holstein-exciton model. By parameterizing the mass asymmetry to decouple it from the small-polaron atomic limit, we map a regime map comprising an internal dressing crossover and a dissociation boundary. We prove analytically and verify numerically that for equal masses, the symmetric exciton ground state is protected from phonon dressing by an exact exchange selection rule, provided the phonon source is odd under electron-hole exchange (the neutral case). As mass asymmetry increases, this selection rule is broken and the exciton acquires a strong local polaronic cloud. We show that the dissociation boundary, conversely, is set by a global energy balance between Coulomb binding and polaronic stabilization, and is nearly independent of the internal dressing. Paradoxically, the very symmetry that protects the exciton from dressing denies it polaronic stabilization, driving it toward dissociation at strong coupling. We discuss these results in the context of lattice exciton-polaron models and their implications for sharp versus broad excitonic lines in mass-symmetric versus mass-asymmetric polar semiconductors.

AI.motivation: In polar materials, a neutral exciton couples to phonons via the sum of electron and hole deformation potentials; charge neutrality makes the total source vanish, so the elastic exciton-phonon vertex is regularized by electron-hole interference. The non-perturbative fate of this interference was previously undetermined.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of a Holstein-exciton model. Mass asymmetry is parameterized to decouple it from the small-polaron atomic limit, yielding a regime map with an internal dressing crossover and a dissociation boundary. Analytical proofs are combined with numerical verification.
AI.result: For equal electron and hole masses, an exact exchange selection rule protects the symmetric exciton ground state from phonon dressing when the phonon source is odd under electron-hole exchange (the neutral case). Increasing mass asymmetry breaks this rule and the exciton acquires a strong local polaronic cloud. The dissociation boundary is governed by a global energy balance between Coulomb binding and polaronic stabilization and is nearly independent of internal dressing.
AI.conclusion: The same symmetry that protects the exciton from phonon dressing also denies it polaronic stabilization, paradoxically driving it toward dissociation at strong coupling. Results are discussed in the context of lattice exciton-polaron models and imply sharp versus broad excitonic lines in mass-symmetric versus mass-asymmetric polar semiconductors.

title: Learning ab initio phase-field models
summary: Simulating microstructure evolution requires quantum-mechanical accuracy and mesoscopic reach in length and time scales, a combination that no current method achieves. Classical phase-field models provide this reach, but their accuracy is limited by phenomenological free energies and mobilities. Here we develop a framework for learning ab initio phase-field models, where the mesoscopic equation is not postulated but derived from a Mori-Zwanzig projection of molecular dynamics onto species-density fields under explicit assumptions. The nonlocal free energy and mobility left unspecified by this equation are parametrized by neural networks and learned from short molecular dynamics trajectories generated with machine-learning interatomic potentials of ab initio accuracy. We demonstrate the framework on an iron-boron melt and on hydrogen-helium mixtures under planetary conditions. For iron-boron, the model shows that the melt at the FeB$_4$ composition is spinodally unstable at ambient pressure but stabilized at 10 GPa, offering a thermodynamic rationale for why FeB$_4$ has been synthesized only under high pressure. For hydrogen-helium, the model predicts the immiscibility boundary and captures droplet nucleation and growth in helium-rain simulations of a column corresponding to 2.2 million atoms, far beyond the scale of atomistic modeling at comparable accuracy. Trained across compositions and conditions, such models could provide a mesoscopic counterpart to ab initio molecular dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework that learns ab initio phase-field models by deriving the mesoscopic equation from a Mori-Zwanzig projection of MD onto species-density fields, parametrizing the unknown nonlocal free energy and mobility with neural networks trained on short MLIP-MD trajectories, and validating it on Fe-B melts and H-He mixtures up to 2.2 million atoms.
AI.motivation: Microstructure evolution simulations require both quantum-mechanical accuracy and mesoscopic length/time reach, a combination no existing method achieves. Classical phase-field models offer the needed mesoscopic reach but suffer limited accuracy due to phenomenological free energies and mobilities.
AI.method: The mesoscopic phase-field equation is not postulated but derived via a Mori-Zwanzig projection of molecular dynamics onto species-density fields under explicit assumptions. The nonlocal free energy and mobility left unspecified are parametrized by neural networks and learned from short molecular dynamics trajectories generated with machine-learning interatomic potentials of ab initio accuracy.
